comment_details.body: I've been able to verify this, and I'm working out a fix for it right now.

I'm working on a solution for this, and in the mean time, you can create a file called `.doctlcfg` in your home directory (not sure what this is on all versions of Windows) with the following contents:

``` yaml
access-token: <your do access token>
```

You can manually retrieve an access token at https://cloud.digitalocean.com/settings/api/tokens

As well, doesn't work with the form of .doctlcfg in the Github Readme.md, unless you put the expected comma in between the arguments, to make it proper JSON.

```
{
    access-token: <yours>,  <---- the crucial comma...
    output: <json|text>
}
```

The location on Win10 and likely earlier is 

```
c:\Users\yourusername_perhapsshortened\.doctlcfg
```

It does work just simply putting 

```
access-token: <yours> 
```

alone in the file, as you suggest above, but better if the full form is used, and the json is actually better for human reading I think.

Few more things to keep in mind
- If droplet B's name is same as droplet A's ID(Unlikely to happen)
- If someone changes name of a droplet or creates a new droplet in web interface.(Add a command to refresh internal droplet id/name cache OR refresh cache when `doctl compute droplet list` is executed)

Something else to note here is that it's completely possible to give a droplet a name that could be identical to a droplet ID (ie. a numeric string).

So it'd probably be safest to explicitly specify that a name is being addressed, eg.:

```
# shutdown droplet with id = 12345678
doctl compute droplet-action shutdown 12345678

# shutdown droplet with name = "12345678"
doctl compute droplet-action shutdown --name 12345678
```

As we move more and more towards tags, we'll start using them for this kind of operations, once APIs move more into this direction we should have a better perspective on this but names are mostly for UI only.

comment_details.body:
MacGyver solution combinding `doctl` access credentials, APIv2, and `jq`

```
curl -s -X GET \
    -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(awk '{print $2}' < ~/.doctlcfg)" \
    "https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/droplets/${machine_id}" | \
        jq -r '.droplet.networks.v4[] | select(.type=="private") | .ip_address'
```

Yes, only the public IPv4 address is easily accessible, but there is still a way:

``` sh
 doctl compute droplet get <dropletID> -o json \
  | jq -c '.[].networks.v4[] | select(.type=="private").ip_address'
```

You don't need curl. The key points here is that every command has JSON output than you can mangle with `jq`

Right, missed the fact that `doctl` provides json output (see my temporary solution above).
Still, would be nice to just have that and not depend on external dependency like `jq`

I think ultimately we shouldn't hardcode every single thing in, but if doctl provided a a way to get at the raw JSON a bit easier, it wouldn't be too bad. Perhaps the easy way would be allow [go template](http://golang.org/pkg/text/template/#pkg-overview), and JSON path support, so you could do something like

`doctl compute droplet get <dropletID> --go-template="whatever"` or
`doctl compute droplet get <dropletID> --jsonpath="whatever"`
Created new issues to add these two features in #95 and #96.

Lists both public and private IP list of all your DO droplets

`doctl compute droplet list -o json |jq -r  '.[]| "\(.id)\t\(.name)\t\(.networks.v4[].ip_address)"'` 


List them in single line

`doctl compute droplet list -o json |jq -r  '.[]| "\(.id)\t\(.name)\t\(.networks.v4[]|select(.type=="public")|.ip_address)\t\(.networks.v4[]|select(.type=="private")|.ip_address)"' `

comment_details.body:
Running this little program will create a bash completion file for doctl.

``` go
package main

import "github.com/digitalocean/doctl/commands"

func main() {
    cmd := commands.Init()
    cmd.GenBashCompletionFile("doctl.sh")
}
```

Save it as `doctl-bash.go` and then with the go compiler installed, you can run it with `go run doctl-bash.go` It will produce a file called `doctl.sh` which you can place in `/etc/bash_completion.d/`

The question is how to best get it in the hands of the user. We could create it as part of the build/release process. Then homebrew (and hypothetical rpms/debs) could install it. An alternative might be to add a new command that does this. For instance, Hugo provides a genautocomplete sub-command.
This is currently on the plate. I'm thinking bash, zsh, and fish (mostly because I use it) for the first version.

For what it's worth I'd suggest generating the completion as part of the build process; then homebrew (or rpm/deb) can just copy it into the right place. (As suggested by @andrewsomething). 

```
$>brew info git
...
==> Caveats

issues.body:
It happens on current master (a57555c), when trying to connect to a droplet from Windows 10 in VirtualBox.

There are 2 different problems:

**1/ When trying to connect with a SSH key that isn't password protected, the error is**:

```
doctl.exe compute ssh playground --ssh-key-path D:\ssh-tmp-keys\id_rsa_without_password
Error: read /dev/stdout: The handle is invalid.
```

The problem is that [this line](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/a57555c195d06bc7aa5037af77fde0665ad1231f/pkg/ssh/ssh_internal.go#L48) is using `os.Stdout` while it should be using `os.Stdin`.

There's also a logical error [here](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/a57555c195d06bc7aa5037af77fde0665ad1231f/pkg/ssh/ssh.go#L83), we check for the _function scoped_ `err` before starting the shell,  but it can be _non-nil_ because of [this line](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/a57555c195d06bc7aa5037af77fde0665ad1231f/pkg/ssh/ssh.go#L67).

**2/ When trying to connect with a SSH key that is password protected, the error is**:

```
doctl.exe compute ssh playground --ssh-key-path D:\ssh-tmp-keys\id_rsa_with_password
Error: asn1: structure error: tags don't match (16 vs {class:1 tag:6 length:50 isCompound:false}) {optional:false explicit:false application:false defaultValue:<nil> tag:<nil> stringType:0 timeType:0 set:false omitEmpty:false} pkcs1PrivateKey @2
```

The problem is that `ssh.ParsePrivateKey(key)` on [this line](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/a57555c195d06bc7aa5037af77fde0665ad1231f/pkg/ssh/ssh_internal.go#L33) expects a [PEM encoded private key](https://godoc.org/golang.org/x/crypto/ssh#ParsePrivateKey) so we have to decrypt it first.

The SSH keys used to reproduce this issue have been generated using:
`ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "t@example.com"`

One key has a passphrase, the other doesn't. They are attached here:
[ssh-test-keys.tar.gz](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/files/380347/ssh-test-keys.tar.gz)

```

Although you can see some information about a droplet being created at the top, the whole usage information is a long enough wall of text for me to not notice that, but to do notice the error at the end. So I was assuming the droplets weren't created, but it turns out that they actually were.

This is caused by doctl first creating the machine, and then running the tag API. As these are [not atomic](https://digitalocean.uservoice.com/forums/136585-digitalocean/suggestions/15593823-allow-setting-tags-when-creating-a-droplet), using a nonexisting tag will not prevent you from creating the droplet. But it's not really obvious that this has happened.

Unless the API is improved, the best fix for the client would probably to verify the tag exists before using them.

Hi,

You must create tag before applying it to droplet.
`doctl compute droplet tag <IDNUM> --tag-name digitalocean` will apply **existing tag** with name `digitalocean` to your droplet.

`doctl compute tag list` will show all available tags you can attach to droplet with Droplet count, e.g. :

```
aaa     0
abb         0
abc         0
bac     0
```

So if you execute `doctl compute droplet tag <IDNUM> --tag-name aaa` it should do it successful, but if you execute `doctl compute droplet tag <IDNUM> --tag-name digitalocean` it will return 404 as `digitalocean` tag doesn't exist.

To create tag you can use command

```
doctl compute tag create sammy
```

Deleting tag could be done by

```
doctl compute tag delete sometag
```

Available tag commands are:

```
Usage:
  doctl compute tag [command]

Available Commands:
  create      create tag
  get         get tag
  list        list tags
  update      update tag
  delete      delete tag

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for tag

Global Flags:
  -t, --access-token string   API V2 Access Token
  -c, --config string         config file (default is $HOME/.config/doctl/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string         output format [text|json] (default "text")
      --trace                 trace api access
  -v, --verbose               verbose output

Use "doctl compute tag [command] --help" for more information about a command.
```

doctl compute droplet create doctl-2 --image 20822342 --region nyc1 --size 20gb --tag-names tag1
```
Yes first is taking string and second can take array but if only one is specified it'll do the same work.

comment_details.body:
Hey @xmudrii, thanks for asking. As you say, `--tag-name` (singular) is very similar to `--tag-names` (plural) except in a few ways:
1. `--tag-name` only accepts one tag.
2. `--tag-name` tag must already exist.
3. `--tag-names` accepts an array of tags.
4. tags in the `--tag-names` array _do not already have to exist_. If any tags in the array are new, we'll create them and apply them to the Droplet. If any tag names in the array already exist, we'll just apply them to the Droplet.

We didn't just outright do away with `--tag-name` because it would be a pretty sudden change, but we'll be deprecating it at some point soon. I highly recommend using `--tag-names` (plural) for the reasons and benefits described above.

Thank you for explanation. I understand now why is it done like that and I agree on it. :)
As I understand it now, I'll close this issue.

issues.body: Documentation unclear on syntax for generating new snapshots

comment_details.body:
Hi there! 
Can I help you with something specific?

**Version 1.5.0 and prior to 1.5.0** have following commands to help you create snapsohts:
## Droplet snapshots
### Creating snapshots
Command for creating snapshots is under `droplet-action` tree — `doctl compute droplet-action snapshot`.
**Syntax is following: `doctl compute droplet-action snapshot <droplet-id> --snapshot-name "some-name"`.**
Once executed, if successful, it'll return snapshot ID and other information:
```
ID		Status		Type		Started At			Completed At	Resource ID	Resource Type	Region
000000000	in-progress	snapshot	2017-01-25 16:35:15 +0000 UTC	<nil>		00000000	droplet		nyc1
```

### Listing snapshots
Command for Snapshots list is under `droplet` tree — `doctl compute droplet snapshots`.
It requires to provide you Droplet ID for which you want to see list of Snapshots. **Syntax is:
`doctl compute droplet snapshots <droplet-id>`.**
Sample output if operation is successful:
```
ID		Name	Type		Distribution	Slug	Public	Min Disk
000000000	test	snapshot	Ubuntu			false	20
```

### Removing snapshots
Command for removing Snapshots is located under `image` command tree — `doctl compute image delete`.
**Syntax is `doctl compute image delete <snapshot-id>`.**
In next step, you should be asked to confirm your intention. To do so, type 'y' and then press 'ENTER'. To skip confirmation you can use `force` flag:
`doctl compute image delete <snapshot-id> --force`.

### Renaming snapshots
Command for renaming is also located under `image` command tree — `doctl compute image update`.
**Syntax is `doctl compute image update <snapshot-id> --image-name "new-name"`.**
If successful, you should see list with that snapshot:
```
ID		Name		Type		Distribution	Slug	Public	Min Disk
000000000	new-name	snapshot	Ubuntu			false	20
```

## Volume (Block Storage) snapshots
**Commands for managing volumes snapshots are not available in version 1.5.0 or older!**

## Future of snapshot commands (development version)

As you can see, there are not in same place so it can be hard to keep up with it. To help users, new commands was implemented. Listing, getting and deleting snapshots is located in new command tree `snapshot`. Executing `doctl compute snapshot` will return you available actions:
```
snapshot is used to access snapshot commands

Usage:
  doctl compute snapshot [command]

Aliases:
  snapshot, s


Available Commands:
  list        list snapshots
  get         get snapshot
  delete      delete snapshot
```

Listing is done by executing: `doctl compute snapshot list`. It'll return list of snapshots for both Droplets and Volumes.
You can also get details of specific Droplet/Volume snapshot by executing: `doctl compute snapshot get <snapshot-id>`.
Deleting is done with: `doctl compute snapshot delete <snapshot-id>`. In next step you are asked to confirm intention. To do so, as already explained, type `y` and then press `ENTER`. Also you can use `--force` flag (and of this version shorthand flag `-f`).

Renaming and creating is where it was before.
Beside that you can also create Volume snapshot with `doctl compute volume snapshot <volume-id>`.
To get this version, you can build `doctl` from source, or wait for next release.

If you need anything more, feel free to ask me anything.

issues.body:
Having to find the fingerprint and provide that to `doctl` is a bit of a pain. It would be a much better user experience if I were able to use the name of my key in the digitalocean interface instead of the fingerprint of the public key in order to identify it. 

i.e this is a bit of a pain:

```
# ssh-keygen -E md5 -lf /path/to/key.pub
2048 MD5:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx foo@gmail.com (RSA)
# doctl compute droplet create --image fedora-25-x64-atomic --region nyc3 --size 16gb --ssh-keys xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx  atomicdroplet
```

this would be better:

```
# doctl compute droplet create --image fedora-25-x64-atomic --region nyc3 --size 16gb --ssh-keys name-of-key  atomicdroplet
```

comment_details.body:
‎‎@mauricio @viola what do you think about this?

I would give this a try if you agree on adding it. Idea seems good and reasonable. Just like you can add SSH keys from Control Panel without worrying about ID/Fingerprint, we can resolve name to preferable option. 

Also, add a new flag, or make it use existing flag?
@xmudrii @dustymabe there is a `ssh key command` to quickly look up ssh key details including the fingerprint: `doctl compute ssh-key list` have you tried that?

@viola - yes. I found that after I fumbled around for a while. This is the 2nd time i've hit this same road block when using doctl and decided to open an issue this time. While having `doctl compute ssh-key list` does help, I think it would be much better to have `--ssh-keys` support names as well.

@dustymabe thank you for the detailed explanation and I'm sorry to hear that you had troubles finding that feature.
@xmudrii while I don't have any objections to this reasonable request I'm afraid that at the moment we don't have a way to look up individual ssh-key via `name` nor we validate for the ssh key name uniqueness when creating one.  It's possible to have two or more keys with diffrent fingerprints and the same name as of now.

@viola @dustymabe Actually I have to agree. Looks like I was typing faster than thinking about it.

For now, we are mostly trying to stick around with IDs (and Fingerprints in SSH Key case). Especially because you can have duplicate names, it's hard to resolve it to ID with absolute precision. It's prone to confusion and errors so sticking to current option is best bet.
‎
With `compute ssh-key list` you can get list of SSH keys and their Fingerprints and IDs. 
If you are highly dependent on it and have any other ideas how to improve and incorporate it, feel free to write down‎, maybe we can help you.

> Especially because you can have duplicate names,

sounds like a bug to me, you fix that and you can fix this :) 

> If you are highly dependent on it and have any other ideas how to improve and incorporate it, feel free to write down‎, maybe we can help you.

Not highly dependent on it, just providing very useful feedback. It would have taken me 5 minutes to get up and running with the `doctl` versus 15. I think that is very valuable feedback to give, so I opened an issue.

@dustymabe ‎Actually, I wouldn't say it's a bug.‎ Many other resources such as Droplets, Volumes, Images (IIRC) allow same behavior. Maybe it sound weird for SSH keys now, but it's not that.
When working with API, ID is usually default property. To make it easier, in last time, there is shift to tagged resources wherever it's applicable. 
‎
If you want to learn `doctl` better, there's a [tutorial](https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/how-to-use-doctl-the-official-digitalocean-command-line-client) explaining most important stuff, you can give it a try. :)

issues.body:
Yes it is possible to --enable-monitoring during machine creation using doctl command.

However, I have a use case where the machine is created in some other manner. And do need a way to enable monitoring using the doctl command on the droplet. 

Can't see this in the documentation. Thanks.

comment_details.body:
@lucidprogrammer No, you can't enable monitoring using `doctl` or API.

You'll have to manually install agent, executing this command on the Droplet:
```bash
curl -sSL https://agent.digitalocean.com/install.sh | sh
```

You can use `doctl compute ssh` to access the Droplet using SSH. You can also try combining it with `--ssh-command` to send command via SSH directly from `doctl`, (_note: `--ssh-command` is not available in `doctl` for Windows_) such as:
```bash
doctl compute ssh droplet-name/ip --ssh-command "curl -sSL https://agent.digitalocean.com/install.sh | sh"
```

Full tutorial on DigitalOcean Agent is available — [How To Install and Use the DigitalOcean Agent for Monitoring](https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/how-to-install-and-use-the-digitalocean-agent-for-monitoring)

comment_details.body:
Hi @suonto,

First of all, there seems to be few errors in the syntax of the command.
`--redirect -http-to-https` should be `--redirect-http-to-https`.
`--health-check protocol :tcp,port:443,check_interval_seconds:20,response_timeout_seconds:10,healthy_threshold:3,unhealthy_threshold:2` have one space more than it should, between protocol and tcp. It should be `--health-check protocol:tcp,port:443,check_interval_seconds:20,response_timeout_seconds:10,healthy_threshold:3,unhealthy_threshold:2`.

At the end, command should be like this:
```

[Previously](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/issues/136), snap support was discussed, and the [yaml](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/master/snap/snapcraft.yaml) is now upstream. We have a snap in the store, which is maintained by our community [snapcrafters](https://github.com/snapcrafters/doctl). 

However we'd prefer that, now you have a yaml in your master branch, we transition the ownership of the snap upstream to you. This should be a fairly painless process, which we can help navigate. Essentially, we need to have:-

  * You register with the snap store at http://dashboard.snapcraft.io/
  * Let us know your account details
  * We request the snap is moved across to your account
  * You hook up our [build service](http://build.snapcraft.io) to push automatically to the store - or you use whatever CI system you prefer to push to the store.

Once you've got an account registered in the store, we can move forward. Do let us know if you have any problems.

Cannot Destroy Space

Any plans to add the ability to configure CDN SSL for spaces with the cli?

@Pagebakers doctl supports configuring Spaces CDNs. It's a bit unintuitive, but you can find those commands under `doctl compute cdn`

To add a CDN in front of a Space, run:

```
doctl compute cdn create foo.sfo2.digitaloceanspaces.com
```

To use a custom domain, you also need to pass the ID of a certificate for the domain:

```
doctl compute cdn create foo.sfo2.digitaloceanspaces.com \
  --certificate-id a112e5bd-5df6-44bc-a6dc-361ac7df730f \
  --domain foo.example.com
```

See https://www.digitalocean.com/docs/apis-clis/doctl/reference/compute/cdn/

It deserves it's own 'spaces' option, but this will do! thanks a bunch.

currently, if I need to bounce my box, I need two commands to reboot 

```
# Find the int ID of the droplet
doctl compute droplet ls | grep "example.com"

# Use the ID above to run command on example.com (id 123456)
doctl compute droplet-action power-cycle 123456
```
This requires one extra step than one would typically expect.

However, most users, I would imagine, only have a few boxes. I'd like to propose another syntax combining these two commands into a single shorthand (commands by hostname):

```
doctl compute droplet-action power-cycle example.com
```
which would be functionally equivilent to the bash command (yes, I know the grep isn't precise, just a rough example):
```
doctl compute droplet-action power-cycle  `doctl compute d ls | grep "example.com" | awk '{print $1}'`
```

When the number of droplets with the hostname of `example.com` = 1, this should introduce no logical issues.

Thoughts?

issues.body:
**Version**

```
doctl version 1.7.1-release
```

**Command**

```
doctl compute volume create storage01-00 --region nyc3 --size 500GB --desc storage01-00
```

**Result**

```
ID                                      Name             Size       Region    Droplet IDs
d17ac8f7-e78f-11e7-bff6-0242ac117a02    storage01-000    465 GiB    nyc3 
```

Only by passing in 536871MB in place of 500GB am I able to get a 500GB volume as expected. This differs from the way the API works in that 500 is an accepted value and conversion isn't required.

**Test - doctl passing MB in place of GB**

```
doctl compute volume create storage01-00 --region nyc3 --size 536871MB --desc storage01-00
```

**Result**

```
ID                                      Name            Size       Region    Droplet IDs
99bc7cdf-e790-11e7-b41a-0242ac113706    storage01-00    500 GiB    nyc3     
```

**Test - API direct**

```
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer [token]" -d '{"size_gigabytes":500, "name": "example", "description": "Block store for examples", "region": "nyc3"}' "https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/volumes"
```

**Result**

```
b8f40965-e791-11e7-b41a-0242ac113706    example                500 GiB    nyc3
```

comment_details.body:
Hello @jonathantittle! :wave: 
This is intended behavior of `doctl` and API. Actually, the problem is that API is not documented properly.

API (and therefore `doctl`) has field `size_gigabytes`. However, [description](https://developers.digitalocean.com/documentation/v2/#create-a-new-block-storage-volume) states that size is in [gibibytes (GiB)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibibyte).

1 gigabyte (GB) is 1000^3 bytes, while 1 gibibyte (GiB) is 1024^3 bytes.
When you're using API, it's assumed that you're providing size in gibibytes. You can also see it in the response—the result is 500 GiB volume.

With `doctl`, you're allowed to specify do you want 500 GB (465 GiB) or 500 GiB.
The correct `doctl` command is:
```
doctl compute volume create storage01-00 --region nyc3 --size 500GiB --desc storage01-00
```
I hope things are cleaner now. If you have any questions feel free to ping me.
Thanks!

issues.body:
Hi All,

Does anyone know how to get a list of all VM droplets into one file?
Ideally, it would be great to get all VMs with the following details:
- Name
- RAM
- Hard Drive
- Created date

Thanks in advance.

comment_details.body:
Hi there,

You can use the output redirection to forward output to the file, for example:
```
doctl some-command > doctl-output.txt
```

To filter down the output and choose only needed columns, you can use the `--format` flag.
For example, the `doctl compute droplet list --format="Name,Memory,Disk,Status"` command would return something along:
```
Name                    Memory    Disk    Status
ubuntu-512mb-nyc3-01    512       20      active
ubuntu-512mb-nyc3-02    512       20      active
```

Append `> output.txt` to the end of the command, to get the `output.txt` file with same content as the above output.

You can also hide headers using the `--no-header` flag:
```
doctl compute droplet list --format="Name,Memory,Disk,Status" --no-header
```
```
ubuntu-512mb-nyc3-01    512    20    active
ubuntu-512mb-nyc3-02    512    20    active
```

This is the plain-text output and therefore, it could be harder to parse it. You can also output the command's result in JSON format, using the `--output` flag:
```
doctl compute droplet list --output=json
```
```
[                        
  {                                                                                                                                                                             
    "id": 78395000,              
    "name": "ubuntu-512mb-nyc3-01",   
    "memory": 512,                      
    "vcpus": 1,                   
    "disk": 20,              
    "region": {   
      "slug": "nyc3",                            
      "name": "New York 3",
...
```
Note that `--format` and `--output=json` flags doesn't work together -- with JSON format you'll always get all fields. You can use some tool such as `jq` to additionally parse it.

Beside `list` command, there's `get` command, which support templates. However, it requires you to explicitly provide Droplet's ID.

For more details on templating and formatting output, check out our Community tutorial, [How To Use Doctl, the Official DigitalOcean Command-Line Client](https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/how-to-use-doctl-the-official-digitalocean-command-line-client#generic-doctl-usage).
If you have any questions, feel free to ping me here and I'll try to help you as much as I can.

comment_details.body:
I think we're gonna need a bit more information into what doctl command you're running and how you're building that. From the error it looks like it's trying to interpret the flag as being the whole thing (`--tag-names stuff,things,bob`) rather than just `--tag-names`.
Can you share some more into how you're building the doctl droplet create command?

The bash command I am using to construct it is `if [ -z "${8}" ]; then DROPLET_TAGS=""; else DROPLET_TAGS="--tag-names ${8}"; fi`

I then pull it into the command as a string using `"$DROPLET_TAGS"`

Because you are quoting the `"$DROPLET_TAGS"` argument, doctl treats the whole string as one argument. You will need it to be split into two. Make sure that your tag names (`${8}`) do not contain any spaces.

```sh
DROPLET_TAGS=""
if [ -n "${8}" ]; then
    DROPLET_TAGS="--tag-names"
    DROPLET_TAGS+="${8}"
fi

This script works so far:

```
#!/bin/bash
# script to create digitalocean droplet snapshot using their CLI, doctl.

# Function to set variable for snapshot name as date/time of creation.
timestamp() {
NAME=$(date)
}

timestamp

doctl compute droplet-action snapshot --snapshot-name "$NAME" 80750079
```
The script works with the result being a droplet snapshot with the date/time of creation as the name. However, I need to keep only 12 snapshots.

Somehow I need to count the number of existing snapshots and when I have 12, delete the oldest and add a new one.

How can I achieve that?

I run the script every two hours.

Thanks!

comment_details.body:
You can get a list of snapshots by running `doctl compute snapshot list`. To limit it to Droplet snapshots only, you can pass `--resource droplet`.

To get a specific Droplet's snapshot, you can `grep` the output for its ID.

```sh
doctl compute snapshot list --resource droplet --format ID,Name,CreatedAt,ResourceId | grep 80750079 | sort -rk 3 | tail +13
```

This command will list all snapshots, filter out any that don't belong to Droplet `80750079`, sort them by date (newest->oldest), and remove lines 1-12. So, it will list all snapshots that you'll want to delete. To get the IDs, pipe the output through `| cut -d' ' -f1`.

`doctl compute snapshot delete` takes snapshot IDs as the arguments. So you can replace the newlines in the above command's output and pass it to that command, like so:

```sh
snapshot_ids=$(doctl compute snapshot list --resource droplet --format ID,Name,CreatedAt,ResourceId | grep 7977406 | sort -rk 3 | cut -d' ' -f1 | tr '\n' ' ')
doctl compute snapshot delete $snapshot_ids
```

You might want to check if `$snapshot_ids` is empty before running the `doctl` command.

Let me know if that helps!

I figured out how to do it this way—please tell me if your method is more advantageous :) I will study your way regardless so I can learn ;)

```bash
#!/bin/bash
exec &> do_snapshot.log

timestamp() {
 NAME=$(date)
}

timestamp

SNAPSHOTS=$(/snap/bin/doctl compute image list-user --format "ID" --no-header | wc -l)

if [ "$SNAPSHOTS" -gt 23 ]; then
mapfile -t IDLIST < <(/snap/bin/doctl compute image list-user --format "ID" --no-header)

OLDEST=${IDLIST[0]}

/snap/bin/doctl compute image delete "$OLDEST"
fi

/snap/bin/doctl compute droplet-action snapshot --snapshot-name "$NAME" 80750079

mail -s "Digital Ocean Hourly Snapshot" donwest.network@gmail.com < do_snapshot.log

rm do_snapshot.log

exit 0
```

(I edited your comment to quote your code with ``` tags)

That also looks good and should work just as fine! Both ways ultimately accomplish the same thing :) I didn't know about the `mapfile` command, that is neat!

Hi there,

Thanks for reporting the issue!

The `format` flags takes column name without spaces, so you usually have to pass something like `--format "ID,DropletIDs"`.

To check out accepted column names, you can execute the appropriate command with the `--help` flag, and it will show you what column names you can provide:

```
doctl compute volume list --help
```
```
list volume

Usage:
  doctl compute volume list [flags]

Aliases:
  list, ls


Flags:
      --format string   Columns for output in a comma separated list. Possible values: ID,Name,Size,Region,Droplet IDs
      --no-header       hide headers
      --region string   Volume region
...
```

However, in case for the `volume list` command, there's a bug, because column names should not contain spaces, or otherwise you'll run into the described issue. I have submitted a pull request to fix this (#322).

issues.body:
Right now we can use the context parameter to create different auth-contexts on the `config.yaml`, which already helps a lot, but I have a few suggestions on top of that:

1) Although stateless has it's advantages, it'd be nice to have an option to modify default behaviour to stateful. 
2) It would be nice to have other settings be context aware, like `compute.ssh.ssh-key-path`, `compute.ssh.ssh-user`, `compute-ssh.ssh-port` and many other things.

The ability to have the option of setting context in a stateful way makes suggestion (2) above make even more sense. You switch the context once and all those settings are already adjusted for you, so no need to be passing them as arguments on the command-line.

comment_details.body: Thanks for the suggestions @rsaffi! Re: 1, you can change the default context using the `doctl auth switch --context new-default-context` command. Does that help?

Hello @kamaln7!

Thanks for the prompt reply! Actually I stand corrected on that. Yes, there's already the possibility of doing a stateful change of context like that; so no need to keep passing `--context=something` on every command.

But I still stand to the fact that it'd be nice to be able to also define some different defaults on the config file per context, like the aforementioned settings, beside others.

I myself use a default ssh user/port/key for my private account but a different one for my company's account and I believe the same probably happens to others.

SSH is just a simple/silly example of what we could benefit with having different defaults for different contexts. But thinking of other defaults (droplet/volumes/dns creation, for instance), there could be great benefits on having this option separate per context.

comment_details.body:
Sorry for the late response here @aheckler. I have a suggestion, let me know if it works for you.

1. Run `doctl auth init` once in order to get a config file.
2. Edit the file and remove all access tokens from it (search for `access-token` and `auth-contexts`). 

Now, you can run any doctl commands while passing the access token using the `DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN` env var with the rest of the config coming from the file which you can commit in git. If you run `doctl auth init` or `doctl auth switch` it will re-write the config file _with_ the access token but you shouldn't need to use these commands.

issues.body:
I access multiple digitalocean account, what is right way to handle it up ?

Currently I copy the original config, change access token and use softlink for point to correct config.
Is there something like profile to access multiple account ?

comment_details.body:
`doctl` supports multiple accounts. The first account configured is known as the `default` To add a new account, you can run:

     doctl auth init --context <account-name>

To switch to that account, run:

    doctl auth switch --context <account-name>

Now all commands will be run using the second account. To switch back to the default account, run:

    doctl auth switch --context default

You can run commands from either account without switching by using the `--context` flag:

    doctl compute droplet ls --context <account-name>

See the README for more info: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl#logging-in-to-multiple-digitalocean-accounts
Thanks for answer, don't know how i missed it.

issues.body:
As the title already says, I'd like to specify a custom `known_hosts` file as I would do with 
```bash 
> ssh -o UserKnownHostsFile=/tmp/known_hosts user@123.123.123.123 
```

Currently the `doctl compute ssh` command does not support this. 

The main reason for this is an automated script that gets the IPs of all current droplets and calls `ssh-keyscan` on each one to avoid this interaction.

```bash
The authenticity of host '123.123.123.123' can't be established. 
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?
```

I would like to use this feature like this in a loop. The interaction of adding the host each time does not really work in that case.

```bash
for my-droplet-name in droplet-names; do
    doctl compute ssh --ssh-known-hosts /tmp/known_hosts \
                      --ssh-command "do stuff here" \
                      $my-droplet-name
done
```

In this case, `/tmp/known_hosts` was filled by another script beforehand.

I'd be willing to create a PR for this, if the feature is wanted. After a quick code check, it looks like it is more or less just passing arguments through the call stack

comment_details.body:
I've started to implement this feature ([WIP here](https://github.com/lawben/doctl)). For unix systems, this is pretty straightforward as we just need to pass the file to the native ssh command. For Windows however (or system that rely on [`ssh_internal`](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/master/pkg/ssh/ssh_internal.go)), a bit of code is needed. There is an official [`knownhosts` module](https://godoc.org/golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/knownhosts) that does most of the heavy lifting, but that currently does not support adding new keys if no matching one was found. So this results in `ssh: handshake failed: knownhosts: key is unknown` at the moment. 

I see three options for this problems:

1. Support known_hosts only on unix systems
2. Write code to add unknown hosts to the provided file, just as unix ssh implementations do with "The authenticity of host xxx can't be established. ECDSA key fingerprint is xxx. Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?"
3. Specify that if a known_hosts file is provided, it must contain the key for the given host or else it will fail.

The third option would suffice for my use case, as I always populate the file with the correct keys beforehand. I guess the second option is the cleanest, as the internal/external ssh commands would then both behave identically, but that means there would be some extra code dealing with adding these hosts. I'd be glad to write this though, if you guys think it's a useful addition.

Please let me know what your thoughts are on this.

issues.title: doctl auth init token validated but error from kubectl

issues.body:
**Actual behaviour / how to reproduce**

When authenticated for the first time with `doctl auth init` it uses the `default` context, which is expected. You can then call `doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig save CLUSTER_NAME` and it will fetch the users/contexts and save it to the kubeconfig.

The issue occurrs once you need to add a second context to doctl, using a command like `doctl auth init --context=everyday` and then wanting to add a cluster from that context to your kubeconfig using `doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig save CLUSTER_NAME2 --context=everyday` 

You would now expect `kubectl cluster-info` to display information about your cluster, but instead it shows an error similar to the following:
`Error: failed to fetch credentials for cluster "37ea18d5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxx": cluster not found`

This is because it still assumes it should use the `default` context, when in-fact the `default` context does not have access to this cluster.

**Expected behaviour / fix**

Expected behaviour would be for the  `doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig save CLUSTER_NAME2 --context=everyday` to pass the context to `exec-credential` in the kubeconfig as shown in the image below:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3168421/58822922-db79e480-8638-11e9-805c-1f7e805faf41.png)

After adding this line everything works fine, even after removing it again for some reason, which I can only assume is because the context the cluster is supposed to have is cached at this point.

This should be a pretty simple fix for anyone familiar with the doctl codebase or Go in particular

comment_details.body: Thanks for a lovely writeup!

@Marcuzz This should be fixed as of [the latest release](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/releases), but please reopen if you have any more issues.

For some more info into the fix, what we do now is ensure that the `--context` string in the your kubeconfig's exec-credential command always contains the exact context that you ran the `doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig save` command with.

Awesome 🥇 

Can confirm that it now works exactly like I wanted it to work. Good work! 😃

issues.body:
**Problem**

When installed as an Ubuntu snap, doctl needs to be explicitly given permission to access SSH keys for use with the `doctl compute ssh` sub-command. For details, see:

https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl#using-doctl-compute-ssh

Attempting to SSH to a Droplet before granting those permissions results in an error:

    Error: fork/exec /usr/bin/ssh: permission denied

Unless you have read the README, this error message can be confusing and does not provide a path forward for the user.

**Proposed Solution**

When `doctl compute ssh` is run in a snap environment (hint: https://docs.snapcraft.io/environment-variables) without first being granted access to the ssh-keys interface, we should catch the permission denied error (or check first if possible) and present the user with an error message with a clear path to resolving the problem. For example:

    Error: fork/exec /usr/bin/ssh: permission denied

    Using the doctl Snap? Grant access to the ssh-keys interface to use this command.

        sudo snap connect doctl:ssh-keys :ssh-keys

~~~command
$ doctl compute volume ls -o json
null

$ doctl compute load-balancer ls -o json
[]
~~~

comment_details.body: @bentranter Feels like we should be able to prevent this sort of error by treating any erroneous nil slices as empty slices in the JSON displaying logic. What do you think?

@hilary I'm not too sure. In our JSON displaying logic, we use `json.Marshal`, and the only option we get there is to either write `null` or nothing in the output, as there's no option for displaying `[]` instead of `null`.

With that said, another approach would be to check each `item` in the `writeJSON` function for any nil slices, and change them to empty slices before calling `json.Marshal`. That would require some pretty heavy use of the `reflect` package though, which I don't think we should get into.

Unfortunately, I think our best bet is to go through each of the commands, and check for cases where we're accidentally returning nil slices. It's the simplest solution, and after briefly looking last week when this issue was reported, I don't think there are too many cases where we do return nil slices.

On a different note, I wonder if fixing this issue qualifies as a breaking change. For example, if there are users who use a tool like `jq` to parse our JSON output, they're probably expecting `null` where we return it, and not `[]`.
But why do I saw `[]` in the load-balancer list?

@fleeto You were seeing `[]` in the load-balancer list due to an inconsistency in the way we rendered empty and nil slices. This is fixed as of [the latest release (1.22.0)](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/releases).

cat <(doctl compute tag list --format "Name" --no-header)

issues.body:
Hi there~

When I'm deleting a floating ip right after it's unassigned from a droplet, the following error occurred:
`Error: DELETE https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/floating_ips/xxx.xxx.xxx.xx: 422 The floating IP already has a pending event.`
The corresponding command is :
```bsah
doctl compute floating-ip-action unassign $OLD_FLIP
doctl compute floating-ip create --droplet-id $DROPLET_ID
doctl compute floating-ip delete -f $OLD_FLIP
```
Inserting a `sleep 10` between the lines is a workaround, yet it *cannot guarantee* that the floating ip is changed successfully.

Is there any safer way to solve this?

Thank you.

comment_details.body:
Unassigning a floating IP returns an action item which can be used to check the the status. Fore example:

```
$ doctl compute floating-ip-action unassign 178.128.133.144
ID           Status         Type           Started At                       Completed At    Resource ID    Resource Type    Region
721743418    in-progress    unassign_ip    2019-07-15 22:00:12 +0000 UTC    <nil>           2994767248     floating_ip      nyc1
$ doctl compute action wait 721743418
ID           Status       Type           Started At                       Completed At                     Resource ID    Resource Type    Region
721743418    completed    unassign_ip    2019-07-15 22:00:12 +0000 UTC    2019-07-15 22:00:13 +0000 UTC    2994767248     floating_ip      nyc1
```

Using `wait` here will block until the action has completed. In a script, you could use something like:

```
ACTION_ID=`doctl compute floating-ip-action unassign --no-header --format ID ${FLOATING_IP}`
doctl compute action wait ${ACTION_ID}
```

Wow cool! That works!
Many thanks for your help!

I am trying to create a load balancer with `doctl` version `1.26.0`, it creates the load balancer, but does not create the HTTPS passthrough rule. Command used:

doctl compute load-balancer create --name example.org-development-swarm-lb --region ams3 --tag-name example_org_development:swarm-node --algorithm round_robin --forwarding-rules entry_protocol:http,entry_port:80,target_protocol:http,target_port:80 entry_protocol:https,entry_port:443,target_protocol:https,target_port:443 --health-check protocol:tcp,port:443,path:,check_interval_seconds:10,response_timeout_seconds:5,healthy_threshold:5,unhealthy_threshold:3

comment_details.body:
Hi @mark-veenstra, to set multiple forwarding rules you must use a quoted string of space-separated values. So that would look like:

```
doctl compute load-balancer create --name example.org-development-swarm-lb \
  --region ams3 --tag-name example_org_development:swarm-node --algorithm round_robin \
  --forwarding-rules "entry_protocol:http,entry_port:80,target_protocol:http,target_port:80 entry_protocol:https,entry_port:443,target_protocol:https,target_port:443,tls_passthrough:true" \
  --health-check protocol:tcp,port:443,path:,check_interval_seconds:10,response_timeout_seconds:5,healthy_threshold:5,unhealthy_threshold:3
```

Note that there is an additional change besides quoting the rules. I've also added `tls_passthrough:true` to the HTTPS rule. When creating an HTTPS rule, you must either specify an SSL certificate ID or enable pass through.

Let us know if you're still running into any issues.
Thanks!

comment_details.body:
@mjclemente I do not think this is an option directly in the `doctl` command, but you could use the JSON output together with `jq`, like so:

**sort on `created_at` ascending**
```
doctl compute droplet list -o json | jq -s '.[] |= sort_by(.created_at)' > output.json
```
**sort on `created_at` descending**
```
doctl compute droplet list -o json | jq -s '[.[]] | sort_by(.[].created_at) | reverse[]' > output.json

```
Above is a retry for cleaning up the same project after the first error. But it errors again now on project deletion. But once logged into the DigitalOcean web interface manually deletion works, so it seems also that some deletions up front are still pending.

Would it be possible to have the `--wait` implemented on all `delete` actions?

comment_details.body:
Thanks for raising this @mark-veenstra. This is a spot where the behaviour between commands is unfortunately a bit inconsistent. We have three different cases,
* The command returns an action ID that we can wait on (for example, something like a volume detach).
* The command doesn't return an action ID, but we can find one. An example here is a Droplet delete, where we can find the corresponding action through `doctl compute action list`.
* The command doesn't return an action ID, and one doesn't exist anywhere.

While there's no quick fix for this, we'll keep this open to track any improvements we make in terms of making these delete operations more consistent.

@murarisumit There currently is no command in `doctl` to list all the contexts. With that said, you can view all of the contexts by viewing your `doctl` config file, typically located at:
* `C:\Users\<your-username>\AppData\Local\doctl\config` on Windows
* Either `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/doctl/config.yaml` or `~/.config/doctl/config.yaml` on Linux and Mac

The contexts appear under the `auth-contexts:` key in the config file.

With that said, I think this would be a useful feature to have, so we'll keep this ticket open to consider adding it.

```

```

comment_details.body:
Hi @gangachris. This is to be expected. When displaying text output, we do not show every attribute available, just a table of certain ones. The `--format` flag can be used to choose which table columns to display as some you might be interested in are hidden by default while others shown by default might not be needed in your case.

    --format string   Columns for output in a comma separated list.

Specifying `-o json` returns the full json output as returned by the API. If you want to display just the id and name attributes in JSON, I'd suggest piping the output to `jq`. For example:

    doctl compute volume list -o json | jq 'map({id: .id, name: .name})'

@andrewsomething Ok. Makes sense. It just feels a little bit unintuitive. Thanks for the explanation.

Closing.

Definetly. We can at least make the help output more clear that format is currently only for text output or perhaps make the arguments mutually exclusive. We'll consider adding support for JSON formatting in the future.

Thanks for the feedback!

There is a problem with initial authentication using following doctl command:
`> doctl auth init`
`DigitalOcean access token: Error: unable to read DigitalOcean access token: The handle is invalid.`

doctl doesn't create config at `\AppData\Local\doctl\config\config.yaml`

Environment:

- doctl 1.30.0 x64 (tried also with 32bit and older versions)
- cmd, cmd run as admin, power shell

comment_details.body: I've reproduced this on a fresh Windows 10 VM, going to look into it now.

Ok, the issue here is that we assume `terminal.ReadPassword(0)` works on Windows. While `0` is the file descriptor for stdin on Unix, it's not on Windows. Updating this to be `terminal.ReadPassword(syscall.Stdin)` should fix it on Go 1.12, but it looks like on 1.13 it needs a type conversion from `syscall.Handle` to `int`. Looking into that now, and then I'll open a PR to fix this.

comment_details.body:
Thanks for reporting this @daohoangson. If installed using snap, doctl has limited access to personal files. It's confined to `~/.config/doctl` (per [snapcraft.yaml](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/master/snap/snapcraft.yaml#L51-L55)) so it can't create the directory `~/.config` if it doesn't exist.

I think this behavior is fine as doctl doesn't need access to all of `~/.config`. We should add a note to the README though.

We'll need snapcraft to update the snap definition for the change to take effect. I'll update `snapcraft.yaml` once the snap definition has been updated.

comment_details.body:
Hey @viorel-anghel,

To create a Droplet in a specific project, you'll need to use an API token for that project. There are two ways to do this.

### Through a CLI argument

doctl allows you to pass a `-t` flag to provide an API access token for that command. For example you could create a Droplet by running

```
doctl compute droplet create <name> -t <project-api-token> --image ubuntu-18-04-x64 --region nyc3 --size s-1vcpu-1gb
```
where,

* `<name>` is the name of the Droplet you want to create (as you probably already know),
* `<project-api-token>` is the API token belonging to the specific project you want to create the Droplet in.

### Using an authentication context

doctl allows you to create named authentication contexts so that you don't need to pass a `-t` flag every time. To do this,

* Run `doctl auth init --context=<project-name>`, where `<project-name>` is the name of your project.
* Provide your project's API token at the prompt.
* Switch to that context by running `doctl auth switch --context=<project-name>`.

Now, anytime you create a Droplet, it will be created using your project's API token until you switch back to your default context. To do that, run `doctl auth switch --context=default`. You can also view the different contexts you've created at any time by running `doctl auth list`.

Hope this helps!

Same question here.

Hi all,

It looks like there was a bit of miscommunication around the different features and terminology. The approach @bentranter describes above is for managing multiple DigitalOcean team or accounts. The DigitalOcean API does not currently support assigning resources to a specific project when the resource is created. Currently, this require a second API call. Using doctl, that command would look like:

    doctl projects resources assign <project-id> --resource=<urn> [--resource=<urn> ...]

The `--resource` flag can be repeated multiple times to assign more than one resource in a single request. It takes a resource's uniform resource name (URN). For a Droplet, that looks like `do:droplet:123456`

See: https://developers.digitalocean.com/documentation/v2/#project-resources

Putting it all together, here's an example of what this might look like in a script:

```
PROJECT_ID="c82f8368-8dc5-45fa-8ffe-28038935f5ce"
DROPLET_ID=$(doctl compute droplet create example.com --size s-1vcpu-1gb --image ubuntu-20-04-x64 --region nyc3 --wait --no-header --format=ID)
doctl projects resources assign ${PROJECT_ID} --resource=do:droplet:${DROPLET_ID}
```

In the Droplet create request, passing `--no-header --format=ID` means that only the ID is printed in response. This allows you to save it into a variable for later use.

Hello,

I want to deploy into a kubernetes cluster from a CD/CI.

For doing that, I'm installing `doctl` and setup an API token with `Read/Write` permissions as `DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN`.

![Screenshot 2019-10-10 at 17 41 33](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2096101/66584337-3c846c80-eb85-11e9-94ba-028e6700dc78.png)

My code looks like

```yml
# installing `doctl`
- DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN=my-read-write-token
- DOCTL_VERSION=$(curl -fsL https://api.github.com/repos/digitalocean/doctl/releases/latest | jq -r ".tag_name" | sed 's/v//')
- curl -fsL https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/releases/download/v${DOCTL_VERSION}/doctl-${DOCTL_VERSION}-linux-amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
- mv doctl /usr/local/bin
# initialize `doctl`
- doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig save my-cluster
```

After that, I execute the command for fetching my cluster configuration, and all is working fine, however, I noted that every time I do that, a new read-only token is generated:

![Screenshot 2019-10-10 at 17 41 36](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2096101/66584351-4312e400-eb85-11e9-8d67-212a252d239d.png)

My question is, essentially, why a read-only token is generated?

How I can avoid that? Why not the process is using the read/write token provided as env variable?

comment_details.body:
You are seeing this due to a recent change in how DOKS Kubernetes clusters handle authentication. Rather than using certificates, they now use API tokens. This gives team administrators much finer control over how their clusters can be accessed. Rather than a shared certificate that can not be revoked, a token tied to a specific kubeconfig file can be revoked without breaking other users.

You can read more about those changes here:

https://blog.digitalocean.com/new-on-digitalocean-kubernetes/
https://www.digitalocean.com/docs/kubernetes/how-to/connect-to-cluster/#automatically-managed-tokens-recommended

If you are able to reuse `~/.config/doctl/cache/exec-credential` across CI runs, only one token will be generated and reused. To prevent the tokens from being generated all together, you can craft a kubeconfig file using a normal DO API token.

```
apiVersion: v1
clusters:
- cluster:
    certificate-authority-data: <CA data>
    server: https://<cluster-id>.k8s.ondigitalocean.com
  name: do-lon1-cluster-name
contexts:
- context:
    cluster: do-lon1-cluster-name
    user: do-lon1-cluster-name-admin
  name: do-lon1-cluster-name
current-context: do-lon1-cluster-name
kind: Config
preferences: {}
users:
- name: do-lon1-cluster-name-admin
  user:
    token: <a DO api token>
```

I've shared this feedback with our Kubernetes team.

issues.body:
I am not sure if I am doing it wrong, but the auth switching feature does not work as expected for me.

### 1. Possible bug: `DIGITALOCEAN_CONTEXT` not working

Following [these instructions][1], I understand that setting the `DIGITALOCEAN_CONTEXT` environment variable is the equivalent of using the `--context <context>` flag.

I expected this to work:

```
$ DIGITALOCEAN_CONTEXT=dannyb doctl account get
```

It does not. The account selected is **not** the one specified in the context.

If this environment variable is only intended to work with the `doctl auth init` command, than

1. it did not work there as well, and
2. it should work across commands. This will allow using some `.envrc` file that can be present on a per-directory basis, and set different contexts without having to type `--context <context>` all the time.

### 2. `doctl auth switch` confusion

Following the pattern of all other commands in the `doctl` CLI, I intuitively typed:

```
$ doctl auth context switch new-context
```

Of course, this does not work (but did not raise an error), as it expects `--context <context>` since it is a global flag.
Since this command is intended to do context switching, I would consider one of these options:

1. Allow this syntax to work: `doctl auth context switch new-context` (this would be my preference. The --context flag should NOT be accepted in this command).
2. Make the `--context` argument mandatory when running this command.
3. Raise an error when running without it, or when running with the extra (ignored) positional parameter, so we know we did something wrong.


[1]: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl#logging-in-to-multiple-digitalocean-accounts

To switch back, run `doctl auth switch --context team_t_context`. If you didn't create a new context for Team T, chances are its context's name is `default`.

Using token [asupersekrettokenthatisverylongidontwanttotypeit]

@zachgersh  do we have any progress/solution ?

@JayKayy I found a custom solution :  https://stackoverflow.com/questions/60221651/doctl-is-unable-to-find-docker-binary/60237742#60237742 
Hope it will help you..

@zachgersh 

I just hit this issue and wrote up my experience debugging it:

https://gist.github.com/gibiansky/f4d7167b67eb88422151ff5d4e5fbf9c

The core issue is that snaps can't access `/usr/bin/docker`, so using `exec.LookPath` to check for Docker via an executable is an issue. I had to get rid of `doctl` snap and install it just as an executable. It seems like there's some sort of special Snap docker support (the `docker` interface / connection) but I couldn't figure out if this would help -- I assume it would let you programmatically act like a Docker client, but still wouldn't let you `exec.LookPath` for the docker executable. 

 It seems like until then just installing Releases from Github is maybe preferred to the the snap install? 

Thanks! Hope my little experience write-up helps someone.

I wanted to provide a bit of an update here: As @gibiansky explained so well, the confinement provided by the Snap security model prevents `doctl` from calling out to the Docker binary. Additionally, the `docker` Snap interface only gives access to the Docker daemon, which does not provide the login mechanism. In order to address this, we have rewritten the command to not depend on the Docker binary being present (see: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/pull/805). This will still require us to get approval from the Canonical Snap team to get write access to the Docker configuration file (`~/.docker/config.json`). We're hopeful that this will be granted.

In the meantime, installing `doctl` directly is a workaround:

https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl#downloading-a-release-from-github

Thanks for the update @andrewsomething.

Will #807 work when `~/.docker/config.json` is only accessible to root? Currently even installing `doctl` directly doesn't work unless the permissions on `~/.docker/config.json` are changed.

@braedon  Unfortunately, if  `~/.docker/config.json` is owned by `root` and `doctl` is run by a non-root user, it will not be able to access the file without changing its permissions. 

You might consider: https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall/#manage-docker-as-a-non-root-user

comment_details.body:
@MarcelHaldimann :wave: 

The snapshot name you specify in the `PersistentVolumeClaim` refers to the _Kubernetes-local_ snapshot object that is expected to be created through a `VolumeSnapshot` object -- it's not directly related to the snapshot name you specify with `doctl compute volume snapshot`.
Since you're already executing the snapshot from within your cluster, is there anything keeping you from periodically executing `kubectl` with [the YAML described in the same document](https://www.digitalocean.com/docs/kubernetes/how-to/snapshot-volumes/#create-a-snapshot-of-a-volume)? That'd be the canonical, Kubernetes-native way to create snapshots.

You could also restore a `doctl`-created snapshot through the cloud control panel and use [our guide](https://github.com/digitalocean/csi-digitalocean/tree/master/examples/kubernetes/pod-single-existing-volume) to import the resulting volume into your Kubernetes cluster. Personally that option wouldn't be my first choice though since you must be careful to follow the guide precisely -- it's easy to accidentally delete your volume if you miss a step. That warning said, both options should work.

Hope this answers your question, but please let us know if not.

comment_details.body:
Hey @sharma-shruti, thanks for the report.

By default, `doctl compute images list` will show only private images. If you don't have any private images, you won't see any output.

If you want to see public images, you'll need to pass the `--public` flag:

```sh
doctl compute image list --public

issues.body:
**What is the problem this feature would solve? Please describe.**
In my pipeline, I get access to my docker registry with the command _doctl registry login_. This generates an API Token, which never expires (oldest is 19 days, so I assume it doesn't expire). For every pipeline run another Access Token is generated, which obviously is a problem over time when it doesn't expire.

I expected the command _doctl registry logout_, in addition to revoke docker's access, to also remove the access token generated. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Have _doctl registry logout_ also remove the access token generated by doctl registry login.

**Additional context**
https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/issues/817

comment_details.body:
As mentioned in #817, doctl v1.44.0 now allows for setting `--expiry-seconds` on the `doctl registry login` command which allows for creating a short lived token that expires, but I'm still going to leave this ticket open.

As the credentials are based on an oAuth token, it might be a good idea to explicitly revoke them on `doctl registry logout` using the normal oAuth call:

https://developers.digitalocean.com/documentation/oauth/#revoke-token-flow

I came here to request this as well. I discovered the `--expiry-seconds` workaround through the CLI help menus, but I think it's safter to explicitly remove the token on logout. I don't always know how long each CI job will take to push new images to the registry. Rather than heavily padding the expiration time, I'd rather just remove the token as soon as it's no longer needed by calling logout.

Through some experimentation, it seems like a `doctl registry logout` followed immediately by a `doctl registry login` will always generate a brand new token. With that in mind, I don't think there's a reason that this can't just be the default action on logout (as opposed to adding an additional flag like `--revoke-token` to the logout command).

comment_details.body:
`doctl auth init` does not generate a token. You must provide one generated in the control panel.

The following commands all generate an API token and each accepts the `--expiry-seconds` argument to produce short-lived tokens:

    doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig save
    doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig saveshow
    doctl registry login

Being able to produce a short-lived token from the control panel something we should support in the future, but that is out of scope for `doctl` itself.

Please feel free to re-open the issue if you feel I've misunderstood it.

comment_details.body:
Hi @anthonysanchezmk ,

How are you adding the credentials to the cluster? The Kubernetes secrets manifest that is created when you run:

`doctl registry kubernetes-manifest | kubectl apply -f -`

specifies the default namespace. Something like:

```
apiVersion: v1
data:
  .dockerconfigjson: REDACEDSECRETS
kind: Secret
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: null
  name: registry-name
  namespace: default
type: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson
```

i'm actually doing it through a git actions. Here is the flow i follow.
https://github.com/do-community/example-doctl-action/blob/master/.github/workflows/workflow.yaml
The `doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig save actions-example-k8s-1-16` command is what i figured where you would configure the namespace, but perhaps I should be doing it earlier?

`doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig save <cluster-name>` doesn't know about namespaces. It provides a kubeconfig file for the a cluster admin user.

In order to pull an image from a private DigitalOcean container registry, you need to first [configure the secret in the cluster](https://www.digitalocean.com/docs/images/container-registry/how-to/use-registry-docker-kubernetes/#kubernetes-integration). This is generally a one time operation. You could do configure this in advance, not as part of the GitHub Actions workflow.

As discussed in the link above, the `doctl registry kubernetes-manifest` command generates a manifest that can be used to configure the secret in the cluster. Though as I mentioned, it is for the default namespace. So you'd need to edit that for your namespace. Something like this should work:

    doctl registry kubernetes-manifest | sed 's/default/<your-namespace>/g' | kubectl apply -f -

We recently released a new feature that should make this even easier. If you are running a DigitalOcean managed Kubernetes cluster, you can automatically add you registry to a cluster with:

```
doctl kubernetes cluster registry add <cluster-id|cluster-name>
```

This only needs to be run once and makes the secret available to all namespaces in the cluster.

comment_details.body:
You need to pass the `--image`  when creating a Droplet. Public images have easy to remember "slugs" that you can reference, e.g.:

```
doctl compute droplet create \
  --image ubuntu-20-04-x64 \
  --size s-1vcpu-1gb \
  --region nyc1 \
  example.com
```

While private images like snapshots must be referenced by ID, eg:

```
doctl compute droplet create \
  --image 34566353 \
  --size s-1vcpu-1gb \
  --region nyc1 \
  example.com
```

You can find the ID's of your snapshots with: `doctl compute image list-user`
Or for public base images: `doctl compute image list-distribution`

Hope that answers your question. Let us know if you have any more!

### Overview

Right now, [Go Report Card](https://goreportcard.com/report/github.com/digitalocean/doctl) reports that we have so gofmt failures in our codebase.

Typically, these can fixed by running `gofmt -s -w ./` from the root of the project.

### How to fix it

1. Clone this repo.
2. If you haven't already, install Go through their [official installer](https://golang.org/dl/).
3. From the root of this project, run `gofmt -s -w ./`. The `-s` flag is short for "simplify", and will make some changes to make the code simpler. The `-w` flag is short for "write", which means that the changes will be written to disk instead of shown in stdout.
4. Open a pull request to this repo with your changes. If you want, mention this issue in your pull request by writing something like, "Closes #866" which will close this issue upon being merged.

I suppose if I had the time, the "right way" (FSVO right way) to fix this would be to clone this to my own GitHub repo, and figure out how to integrate it into SUSE's OpenBuild Service to build RPM and DEB packages and just make my own personal apt & zypper repos. (That sounds like an awful lot of work for a tool that I have never even used due to this open issue.)

Fair point, an already installed local container runtime environment is helpful in this case. However, since "doctl" is a tool from a cloud service provider, an already installed container runtime environment seemed very likely to me. On top of that, the current container image is just about 18MB in size. With a simple alias, it is possible to achieve a comparable user experience in this way with a very reasonable amount of time. For these reasons, I think the atomic bomb comparison is a bit exaggerated.
Best regards,
bdb

I've seen a similar thing.  It works just fine when I run my bash script directly (as a user, or as root).  But when triggered by systemctl it is failing.

My solution to it was:
```
# When running the script from the systemd service, it weirdly doesn't allocate a $HOME variable, which the doctl tool requires.
# Assuming we running as root, but really dont need to (but what other default account should we set the service to use?)
[[ -z "$HOME" ]] && export HOME=/root
```

adding that at the top of my script fixed the problem and it was able to work fine after that.

(I should also mention, it was running fine as a systemctl service on my original server, but only had this problem on a new replacement server... so assuming something else might be missing on the new server but haven't been able to identify it... everything else working just fine so far, just this oddity)

Your issue is completely different. This report concerns the Snap app failing to run when called interactively from the shell. I have no idea if this problem still exists since I gave up on doctl three years ago when I submitted this report.

**Describe the Issue:**

<!-- Please provide a clear and concise description of the problem you are
facing including the steps to reproduce the issue. -->

We trying to use the zsh completion generated by doctl with a sed version not supporting the `_filedir` extension (so busybox sed, that is used by default on alpine linux)


**Environment:**
<!-- Please provide the following information: -->
 - doctl version:
both the last release:
```doctl version 1.52.0-release
Git commit hash: af5bae4
```
and the one packaged on alpine:
```
doctl version 0.0.0-dev
```
 - OS: alpine linux edge and 3.1.12
 - Installation method: using the [distribution package](https://pkgs.alpinelinux.org/package/edge/testing/x86_64/doctl) and downloading from [the release page](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/releases/tag/v1.52.0).

**Additional Details:**
Here is a detailed how to to reproduce the bug. It assumes you have docker installed and running, and your containers can access internet.

### Running a clean alpine container with docker:
`docker run -it alpine /bin/sh`

### Setup in the container
```shell
# apk add zsh
# zsh
# autoload -Uz compinit
# compinit
# wget https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/releases/download/v1.52.0/doctl-1.52.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz
# tar -C /usr/local/bin -zxvf doctl-1.52.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz
```

The bug in itself
```shell
# source <(doctl completion zsh)
```

You should get the following output
```
sed: bad regex '[[:<:]]_filedir[[:>:]]': Unknown character class name
```

Note: If we used the alpine provided [doctl-zsh-completion](https://pkgs.alpinelinux.org/package/edge/testing/x86_64/doctl-zsh-completion) package, the same bug would appear when trying to use the autocomplete (ie, `doctl [tab]`)


It seems the bug comes from [line 600 of the completion.go file](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/5d55b2d49a8bc47043d64c5ccd6f879c6cf10535/commands/completion.go#L600).
issues.title: zsh autocompletion uses non portable sed extensions

**Describe the Issue:**

See: https://www.digitalocean.com/community/questions/how-to-update-dns-records-receiving-data-needs-to-end-with-a-dot

The issue is in the API but is surfaced through `doctl` too:

```bash
doctl compute domain records update ${DOMAIN} \
--record-id ${ID} \
--record-ttl 43200

Error: PUT https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/domains/.../records/...: 422 Data needs to end with a dot (.)
```

The workaround works when applied to `doctl` too (adding `--record-data`):

```bash
doctl compute domain records update ${DOMAIN} \
--record-id ${ID} \
--record-ttl 43200 \
--record-data "${DATA}."
```

```
Error: DELETE https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/vpcs/5570051f-dc85-11e8-9f23-3cfdfea9fff1: 403 (request "f98031a7-df68-40b2-939b-a698f811543d") Can not delete default VPCs

As the error message returned by the API points to, you can not delete a VPC while it is a region's default. In order to delete it, you first must another set another in the same region to be the default:

    doctl vpcs update <vpc-id> --default

or via the control panel: https://www.digitalocean.com/docs/networking/vpc/how-to/set-default-vpc/

> I don't think I completely understand the meaning of 'Can not delete default VPCs'. It thought it seems that the VPC's aren't being assigned to a project, but being created in the global namespace?

VPCs do not live in a project. Projects are mostly just for organization while VPCs define networking. You can have a resources from multiple projects that are in the same VPC.
Ohh, I understand now, thankies for the clarification!
No problem!

issues.body:
**What is the problem this feature would solve? Please describe.**
Now, `doctl` after auth init action, saves long-lived token for DO resources in a file system (config file).

**Describe the solution you'd like**
`doctl auth` should allow bypass the local storage and get the desired token from Vault repository. In that case, short-lived Vaults tokens will allow to getting long-lived. Similar features are available in terms of shadowing secrets on well-known cloud providers as with the AWS, Azure etc.
 
So the desired scenario might look like:
1. Call `doctl auth init` for getting Vault connection properties.
2. Call `vault login` in order to login into Vault (e.g. via OIDC provider, GitHub etc.)
3. Use `doctl` as usual, but in the background, `doctl` uses Vault client and honoured the default token from `~/.vault-token` in terms of getting target DO token.

**Additional context**
This suggestion improves significantly security in case of using `doctl` on the desktop env. It avoids storing DO tokens locally on fs.

**Describe the Issue:**

`doctl apps` ignores the global `envs` section of the appspec file. It's misleading when using `doctl apps spec get ${APP_ID}` when the generated appspec file is missing these values, but can be catastrophic when using `doctl apps update ${APP_ID} --spec app.yaml` as this ignores the values in the appspec file and removes all existing global envs from the application.

The global `envs` section is present when exporting the appspec through the gui.

**Environment:**
 - doctl version 1.54.0-release
Git commit hash: a901a727
 - OS: Ubuntu 20.04.1 LTS
 - Installation method: Snap package

comment_details.body: Thanks for the report. App platform global envs are a new feature that is not yet supported in `doctl`. Looks like we'll need to cut a new godo release with the changes from https://github.com/digitalocean/godo/pull/422 and rebuild doctl with that.
Thanks for the quick response and a quick fix!

comment_details.body:
Hi @MihkelBaranov. Thanks for the suggestion! We'll want to make sure we end up with a solution that works well with what the App Platform team has planned. In the meantime, it seems like this could be scripted. Something like this might work as part of a CD pipeline:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -e

if [ $# -ne 2 ]; then

comment_details.body:
Hi there, thanks for bringing this up.

The short and sweet answer here is that there is a work around. `doctl registry login` is just a bit of a convenience. You can login to a DO registry without it via `docker login -u $DO_TOKEN -p $DO_TOKEN registry.digitalocean.com` more info [here](https://www.digitalocean.com/docs/container-registry/how-to/use-registry-docker-kubernetes/#docker-integration).

Now, to dig a little deeper into the perceived behavior- snap is designed to work in strict confinement and only access things (directories, services, etc.) that they have been granted permission for. This works great when they need access to well-defined common things like networking, a camera interface, etc. It's a bit like installing an app on a cell phone. It gets difficult when two arbitrary applications need to interact. There's a related issue on the Docker side that could provide some more info [here](https://github.com/docker-snap/docker-snap/issues/7)

Very helpful, thank you!

I like the principle of the containment from using Snaps but, to your point, sometimes using them bite me.

### Describe the Issue:

With one or more auth contexts that are email addresses (eg `test@example.com`), using `doctl auth switch` mangles ALL `auth-contexts` keys in the config file: it removes the TLD substring (eg `com`) from each original email address key, and makes it a "sub key" under the now-mangled email address key:

A `~/.config/doctl/config.yaml` with working contexts/API keys:
```
auth-contexts:
  test@example.com: my_secret_api_key
  test2@example.org: another_secret_api_key
```

The same `~/.config/doctl/config.yaml`, after a `doctl auth switch`:
```
auth-contexts:
  test@example:
    com: my_secret_api_key
  test2@example:
    org: another_secret_api_key
```
----
### Steps to reproduce:

1. Just showing I am doing this from scratch:
```
$ rm -rf ~/.config/doctl/config.yaml

$ doctl auth list
default (current)
```

2. Run a `doctl auth init` and verify the new context:
```
$ doctl auth init --context "test@example.com"
Please authenticate doctl for use with your DigitalOcean account. You can generate a token in the control panel at https://cloud.digitalocean.com/account/api/tokens

Enter your access token:
Validating token... OK

$ doctl auth list
test@example.com
default (current)
```

3. Run a `doctl auth switch` (with or without arguments; this will mangle ALL auth contexts that are email addresses)
```
$ doctl auth switch
Now using context [default] by default

$ doctl auth list
test@example
default (current)
```

----

I assume this is happening [somewhere around here](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/00cddfcca309bdb8c5fb46b5399218ceae39a28b/commands/auth.go#L234), so not 100% sure it's a `doctl` thing, or upstream `gopkg.in/yaml.v2` / `spf13/viper` issues.
