issues.body:
**What is the problem this feature would solve? Please describe.**
For an application I'm building I would like to have a GitHub action temporarily connect to a database to perform some migrations. The machine that the action runs on is going to be one of many different machines with an IP address that's hard to know ahead of time. I would like to add the ip address rule tag temporarily, execute the migration, then remove it.

Adding the rule is straightforward and can be done with the following github action YAML:

```yaml
  - name: Determine Public IP
    id: ip
    uses: haythem/public-ip@v1.2

  - name: Allow GitHub CI Runner
    run: doctl databases firewalls append ${{ secrets.DO_FW_ID }} --rule ip_addr:${{ steps.ip.outputs.ipv4 }}
```

The output of this command looks something like this:

```
UUID      ClusterUUID  Type     Value
UUID_1    DB_ID_1    ip_addr    1.2.3.4
UUID_1    DB_ID_1    ip_addr    AA.BB.CC.DD
UUID_1    DB_ID_2    ip_addr    10.XX.XX.XX/XX
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Unfortunately, scripting a solution to then remove the rule is quite a bit more complex. One needs to grep the output from the previous command searching for an occurrence of the IP that was provided as input, sed/awk out the first column, assign that value somehow to another variable, and use it later for the removal command.

What would be convenient is if the `remove` subcommand was symmetrical to the `append` subcommand. For example, the following would be straightforward to implement (and also be more intuitive--it's the first thing I reached for):

```yaml
  - name: Disallow GitHub CI Runner
    run: doctl databases firewalls remove ${{ secrets.DO_FW_ID }} --rule ip_addr:${{ steps.ip.outputs.ipv4 }}
```

**Additional context**
I believe the functionality was added in #950. In that PR the author even hinted that the `remove` command would follow the `doctl databases firewalls remove --rule type:value` pattern.

I do see that it's possible to have duplicate tags (like `ip_addr:1.2.3.4` repeated twice), which is perhaps the reason why a UUID is used for removal instead of the tag. That said, I believe adding the `remove --rule` flag and have it remove all repeated rules would be the desired behavior. This is kind of like comparing the linux `kill PID` command (analogous to the `--uuid` flag) with the `killall COMMAND` command (analogous to the proposed `--rule` flag), where different scenarios requires one or the other.

comment_details.body:
Thanks for bringing this to our attention @tlhunter. We'll have to look into adding the functionality you describe. We're also open to reviewing PRs if you have time to contribute.

Meanwhile, I'd like to offer a workaround so you can get your workflow in place until we can get the functionality properly implemented. Since doctl commands can format output as json (`doctl dbs fw ls <db-uuid> -o json`), that output can be piped to other tools like jq, which is already available to github workflows. 

I just tried this command and was able to delete a rule by IP address value without knowing the rule uuid first:

`doctl dbs fw remove $DB_UUID --uuid $(doctl dbs fw ls $DB_UUID -o json | jq -cr '.[] | select ( .value == "$FW_RULE_IP_VALUE") | .uuid')`

You'll just need to make sure the workflow populates the appropriate environment variables or customize this command to fit your needs.

Thanks, @scotchneat, the `-o json` flag worked like a charm.

While GitHub does offer the ability to [extract output variables from shell scripts](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflow-commands-for-github-actions#setting-an-output-parameter), I actually didn't need it since the list and remove can be performed in the same step.

Feel free to close this ticket if you'd like, though I suspect it would still be a beneficial feature. I probably won't have the spare time to tackle a PR for a few months.
That's great to hear @tlhunter. Please don't hesitate to reopen this request for further discussion.

comment_details.body: This is the behavior for all boolean flags. `--droplet-agent` by itself means `true`, and `--droplet-agent=false` is needed to disable it. We inherit this from Cobra, the library we use for flags, but it is also the behavior for the `flag` package in the Go standard library. We should find a way to make this more clear in the documentation.

I consulted the man page with `doctl compute droplet create -h` so, including the equal sign there should be sufficient. I hope there are not too many other places in doctl that require boolean arguments...

**Environment:**

 - OS: Ubuntu 21.04

169333525    A       foo     192.168.1.2    0           0       1800    0

# Updating the record requires specification of the desired TTL to maintain its value
$ doctl compute domain records update $ZONE --record-id 169333525 --record-data 192.168.1.2 --record-ttl 600
ID           Type    Name    Data           Priority    Port    TTL    Weight
169333525    A       foo     192.168.1.2    0           0       600    0

# Patch the source for doctl changing the default TTL on updates from 1800 to 0
$ git diff
diff --git a/commands/domains.go b/commands/domains.go
index d5ac511b..24936095 100644
--- a/commands/domains.go
+++ b/commands/domains.go
@@ -84,7 +84,7 @@ func Domain() *Command {

        AddIntFlag(cmdRecordUpdate, doctl.ArgRecordPriority, "", 0, "Record priority")
        AddIntFlag(cmdRecordUpdate, doctl.ArgRecordPort, "", 0, "The port value for an SRV record")
-       AddIntFlag(cmdRecordUpdate, doctl.ArgRecordTTL, "", 1800, "The record's Time To Live value, in seconds")
+       AddIntFlag(cmdRecordUpdate, doctl.ArgRecordTTL, "", 0, "The record's Time To Live value, in seconds")
        AddIntFlag(cmdRecordUpdate, doctl.ArgRecordWeight, "", 0, "The weight value for an SRV record")
        AddIntFlag(cmdRecordUpdate, doctl.ArgRecordFlags, "", 0, "An unsigned integer between 0-255 used for CAA records")

# Build

169333525    A       foo     192.168.1.2    0           0       600    0
```

comment_details.body: This was introduced in https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/commit/21279c8c5ab687508ec9130d5a7aa5695b460bfb then the TTL option was initially added.

Thanks for bringing up this issue. You'll see that we've pushed up a PR for this issue #1027 . Once this PR is included in the latest doctl release, you'll need to do one more work around to get the expected behavior. The work around involves editing your doctl config file. Your doctl config file is located in different directories depending on your OS- you can see where your doctl config is located [here](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl#configuring-default-values). Once you've located your doctl config file, edit the records.update.record-ttl from 1800 to 0, as shown below:
```
records:
  create:
    format: ""
    no-header: false
    record-data: ""
    record-flags: 0
    record-name: ""
    record-port: 0
    record-priority: 0
    record-tag: ""
    record-ttl: 1800
    record-type: ""
    record-weight: 0
  delete:
    force: false
  list:
    format: ""
    no-header: false
  update:
    format: ""
    no-header: false
    record-data: ""
    record-flags: 0
    record-id: 0
    record-name: ""
    record-port: 0
    record-priority: 0
    record-tag: ""
    record-ttl: 0
    record-type: ""
    record-weight: 0
```

This will get you the expected behavior.

@arycloud, I wouldn't be able to test your exact compose file without access to the context of your code but I tested the process using my own compose file and was able to successfully push the images.

I did notice the images referenced in your compose file are missing the repository name. The proper syntax should be `<registry>/<repository>:<tag>`. In your compose file, `registry.digitalocean.com/pythonist-do:web` and `registry.digitalocean.com/pythonist-do:nginx-proxy` look like you have the repository in the tag location. 
Your registry is `registry.digitalocean.com/pythonist-do`, and that should be the same thing you get if you run `doctl registry get`. The images should look something like `registry.digitalocean.com/pythonist-do/web:0.1.0` (where `:0.1.0` indicates the tag for the `web` repository).

However, those differences shouldn't cause the error you're receiving. So, to diagnose your issue further, can you answer the following:
* After you confirm doctl is using the auth context you want, are you using doctl to login to your account's container registry? You would do this by running `doctl registry login`.
* Once you're logged in, and before you attempt to push the images, are you building the images in the compose file? You would need to run `docker-compose -f docker-compose.staging.yml build .` (assuming the compose file is in the same directory as the app)

If you've logged into your container registry successfully, and you still receive the same error, the following information will be helpful to further diagnose the issue:

What version of docker are you using (run `docker version`)?
What version of `docker-compose` are you using (run `docker-compose version`?

I'm going to go ahead and close this one out. If you're still running into issues, please feel free to reopen.

For the record, I believe that the root of the issue is in fact the missing the repository name that @scotchneat mentioned. There are a few related upstream issues for Docker:

* https://github.com/distribution/distribution/issues/2649

**Describe the Issue:**

I ran the `kubeconfig` save command within the terminal in my Goland IDE:

```
doctl kubernetes cluster kubeconfig save <id>
```

When my kubeconfig was modified, it used `goland` as the executable instead of `doctl`. This caused any usage of that cluster to open goland with a bunch of empty files:

```yaml
- name: <name>
  user:
    exec:
      apiVersion: client.authentication.k8s.io/v1beta1
      args:
      - kubernetes
      - cluster
      - kubeconfig
      - exec-credential
      - --version=v1beta1
      - --context=default
      - <id>
      command: goland
      env: null
      interactiveMode: IfAvailable
      provideClusterInfo: false
```

I haven't looked at the source, but I imagine it's using the executable name from `os.Args`, which is likely being modified by the goland terminal. It must be passing all commands through `goland` first. 

I assume the reason for doing this is so that someone can rename the `doctl` executable, but perhaps that should just be hard-coded instead.

comment_details.body: Just tried to reproduce this on MacOS using the same `doctl` installation method. Works as expected there, so it looks like we'll need to try to reproduce it on Ubuntu.

@davidsbond How did you install Goland? Could you also share the results of `$SNAP_NAME` returned in the Goland terminal?

The code that determines the name of the executable in `doctl` that would set the executable name in the kubeconfig is this:

https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/57879e2e3e4c66eab7610722bb969fa1d85642cc/doit.go#L502-L509

So that suggests that the `SNAP_NAME` environment variable is the most likely culprit.
Update: another engineer on our team tried to install Goland through the Snap store (https://snapcraft.io/goland) on Ubuntu, and wasn't able to reproduce, so perhaps that's not the issue here.
That looks like the culprit, when I do `echo $SNAP_NAME` within my goland terminal I get `goland` back. To install goland via snap I'm pretty sure I just did `snap install --classic goland`

```
goland                      2021.2.3                    151    latest/stable    jetbrains✓    classic
```

From `snap list`

Ah okay perfect, thanks. Another member of our team just managed to reproduce it as I was typing my earlier update.

It looks like when `goland` is installed through the Snap store, but `doctl` isn't, the embedded Goland terminal has `SNAP_NAME` set to `goland`. If you install `doctl` through the Snap store as well, the `SNAP_NAME` variable is set to `doctl` which fixes the issue.

We can probably add a special case in our environment variable detection here for your use case. I'll work on a pull request. Thanks for your help solving this @davidsbond!

runc is a CLI tool for spawning and running containers on Linux according to the OCI specification. In runc, netlink is used internally as a serialization system for specifying the relevant container configuration to the `C` portion of the code (responsible for the based namespace setup of containers). In all versions of runc prior to 1.0.3, the encoder did not handle the possibility of an integer overflow in the 16-bit length field for the byte array attribute type, meaning that a large enough malicious byte array attribute could result in the length overflowing and the attribute contents being parsed as netlink messages for container configuration. The main users impacted are those who allow untrusted images with untrusted configurations to run on their machines (such as with shared cloud infrastructure). runc version 1.0.3 contains a fix for this bug. As a workaround, one may try disallowing untrusted namespace paths from your container. comment_details.body:
Hi @lukasleuschen,

The image published to Docker Hub uses `doctl` as the entrypoint. This is designed so that it can be used on the command line like:

```
docker run --rm --interactive --tty \
  --env=DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN=<YOUR-DO-API-TOKEN> \
  digitalocean/doctl account get
```

Inside the container itself, the `doctl` binary is installed to the `/app` directory which is set as `WORKDIR`. It is not added to the `PATH`. If you want to use in a derived image, you'll need to do something like:

```
FROM digitalocean/doctl
RUN ./doctl version
```

Hey @andrewsomething 
thank you so much for responding so quickly. Is there a certain reason that doctl isn't in PATH? I can't be the only one trying to build a runner that can interface with DOs managed kubernetes? Or is this not the image one is supposed to use for such things?

Generally, we built this image with `docker run` as the expected usage, but we've definitely seen people using it as a base image. We can consider adding it to `PATH`, but installing it to somewhere besides `/app` would be a breaking change as we see people referencing the full path to it. For example, people are copying over the binary to their image with:

    COPY --from=digitalocean/doctl /app/doctl /bin/doctl
Personally, I think it would be great to add it to `PATH` because the suggested method of installation via `snap` (from the official documentation) doesn't seem to work in a docker image

Hi,

I'm trying to use `doctl apps update --wait` in a continuous deployment pipeline. Sometimes this works fine, other times the command hangs until max attempts. Looking at the source, I think I can see the problem.

https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/62602dba745d478962fa029f2d2a2c61bb4f93e0/commands/apps.go#L352-L355

This is where the `wait` flag is applied. `waitForActiveDeployment` is called with an empty string as the deployment ID.

https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/62602dba745d478962fa029f2d2a2c61bb4f93e0/commands/apps.go#L452-L460

Inside `waitForActiveDeployment`, if the deployment ID is empty the app is fetched and `deploymentID` is set from the `InProgressDeployment` **if it's non-nil**.

However, what I can see if I hit the `update` command a few times is that sometimes `in_progress_deployment` isn't set right after updating, presumably when there are no changes to make. When this is the case, `update --wait` will loop for `maxAttempts` since `deploymentID` will remain `""` and `app.InProgressDeployment.ID` will remain `nil`.

I'm not too sure of the semantics of the DO API, but the response doesn't seem to include anything that could strictly correlate to the update. If the `update` response could be assumed to contain the `InProgressDeployment` if it's not a no-op, then it might work to only call `waitForActiveDeployment` if `app.InProgressDeployment != nil`, and pass long the `DeploymentID` otherwise.

DOKS node pools default to three nodes. As you did not explicitly add a `count`  argument, the default is used. Though with auto-scaling enabled and no active workloads, it scales back down to two.

**What is the problem this feature would solve? Please describe.**

Currently there aren't any examples showing what a path should look like. Does it start with a leading slash? Do you need the bucket name like you do in s3cmd? Can you start with a wildcard to flush everything with a given file extension?

The fact that doctl always returns an empty success makes it even more difficult to determine whether you've entered the path correctly.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Documentation showing a few examples of how you'd format a request, like:

```
doctl compute cdn flush <cdn-id> [/spacename/foldername/*]
doctl compute cdn flush <cdn-id> [*/*.mp4]
doctl compute cdn flush <cdn-id> [/spacename/*.obj]
```

It would be great if doctl could also return a list of the files that had their cache flushed.

Thanks!

comment_details.body: Hey @andrewsomething can i take up this ?
@rustiever  Go for it! Let me know if you need any pointers.
hey i would love to have some pointers to get started @andrewsomething

Hey @rustiever!

The  `doctl compute cdn flush` command is constructed here:

https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/76730b59c7349b665466ebbd687662709acd1baf/commands/cdns.go#L82-L92 

You can make updates to the help output there. Next, you can run `make build`. That will build a version of `doctl` with your changes in the `builds/` directory. You can check that your changes look as expected by running the command from the new build:

    ./builds/doctl compute cdn flush -h

Wildcards can only be used to recursively purge a folder, e.g.  `/spacename/foldername/*` or all files `*`, not for matching patterns ( `/spacename/*.obj`). So some example commands could be:

    doctl compute cdn flush <cdn-id>  --files /path/to/assets/*
    doctl compute cdn flush <cdn-id>  --files "/path/to/file.one, /path/to/file.two"
    doctl compute cdn flush <cdn-id>  --files /path/to/file.one --files  /path/to/file.two
    doctl compute cdn flush <cdn-id>  --files *

Dependency Hierarchy: - github.com/docker/cli-v20.10.14 (Root Library) - github.com/moby/moby-v20.10.17 - :x: **github.com/opencontainers/runc-v1.1.0** (Vulnerable Library)

Vulnerability Details

runc is a CLI tool for spawning and running containers on Linux according to the OCI specification. A bug was found in runc prior to version 1.1.2 where `runc exec --cap` created processes with non-empty inheritable Linux process capabilities, creating an atypical Linux environment and enabling programs with inheritable file capabilities to elevate those capabilities to the permitted set during execve(2). This bug did not affect the container security sandbox as the inheritable set never contained more capabilities than were included in the container's bounding set. This bug has been fixed in runc 1.1.2. This fix changes `runc exec --cap` behavior such that the additional capabilities granted to the process being executed (as specified via `--cap` arguments) do not include inheritable capabilities. In addition, `runc spec` is changed to not set any inheritable capabilities in the created example OCI spec (`config.json`) file.

comment_details.body:
The problem here is with `snap`.   I have been able to reproduce the problem.   The install step succeeds completely and a subsequent check shows that all the components have installed correctly.   For example, if I explicitly type `/home/.../.config/doctl/sandbox/node` at a terminal prompt, it executes just fine.   But, I believe the confined environment that `doctl` is running in when installed by `snap` simply does not permit executing binaries outside the confined area.   I also looked at all the `snap` permissions and didn't see one that would affect executing binaries.   Most of the `doctl sandbox` commands require this.

I also tried uninstalling and reinstalling with the `--classic` flag.   Supposedly, this allows the binary to be installed in an "unconfined" way.   But, this capability has to be enabled by the packager (that's us, at DigitalOcean) and I have not yet had a chance to explore whether this is an option.

I think the immediate bottom line is
- the sandbox commands will not work with a `snap` install of `doctl`.    Doing a direct download from the release site https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/releases is the only current path for linux users
- this is our bad: our testing covered only the direct download cases (lesson learned)
- I don't know of a workaround but hope others might
- meanwhile, we'll work to fix this transparently (if possible) or at least support `--classic` installs.

There is actually a workaround while continuing to use `snap` to install.
```
snap remove doctl
snap install doctl --devmode
```
Starting with point release 1.76.1, `doctl sandbox install` will detect that it is running in a Snap and will make this suggestion.

We're thinking about a better fix, but we can't give a timetable yet.

We've just release version 1.76.2 which should resolve this issue and allow for the `doctl sandbox` commands to work as expected without needing to use `--devmode`.  To upgrade to the new release, run:

    sudo snap refresh doctl

This is accomplished by shipping the sandbox environment along side `doctl` in the Snap package. Now when installed as a Snap, you will no longer need to run `doctl sandbox install` and can proceed directly to calling `doctl sandbox connect`

Thanks again for flagging this for us, and let us know if you run into any other issues.

Closed via https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/pull/1173

<!-- A clear and concise description of what you want to happen. -->

I have a library to zip the contents of `node_modules` and minify the files called [node_modules_packer](https://github.com/H4ad/node-modules-packer) and I want to use this library to create a zip file and then upload it to Functions.

Serverless Framework has a solution called [artifact](https://www.serverless.com/framework/docs/providers/aws/guide/packaging#artifact), which looks like:

```yml
package:
  artifact: path/to/my-artifact.zip
```

So the solution I wanted was something like:

```yml
packages:
  - name: sample
    functions:
      - name: hello
        file: 'path/to/my-artifact.zip'
        zipped: true
        main: ''
        runtime: 'nodejs:18'
        web: true
```

**Additional context**
<!-- Add any other context about the feature request here. -->

I spent a couple hours reading the source code of this CLI my discovers was: `doctl` call [@nimbella/nimbella-cli](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@nimbella/nimbella-cli), and then call [@nimbella/nimbella-deployer](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@nimbella/nimbella-deployer).

The `@nimbella/nimbella-deployer` has support to deploy the content of the Function as zip file [here](https://github.com/nimbella/nimbella-deployer/blob/4841ca48f49ea1ce9244906294a6e35298469c75/src/deploy-struct.ts#L62) and [here](https://github.com/nimbella/nimbella-deployer/blob/4841ca48f49ea1ce9244906294a6e35298469c75/src/deploy-struct.ts#L57).

In theory, it already has support for deploying zip files but `docl` doesn't enable this functionality.

comment_details.body:
I believe the stated goal can already be achieved without changes to `doctl` or the `nimbella` libraries.    The only restriction is that either
1. the build to run `node_modules_packer` must run in the `packages/sample/example` directory, or 
2. it must run somewhere off the `lib` directory (where `lib` is a peer of `packages`) or 
3. it must run external to the project structure before `doctl sls deploy` is. called but deposit the resulting zip file either in `packages/sample/example` directory or somewhere under `lib`.

The structure for (1) is
- project.yml
- packages
  - sample
    - example
      - build.sh
      - (any other files you need for your build)
      - .include

where the file `.include` contains a single text line with the path to your zip file, which must not be absolute or. contain `..` directives (ie, the file must end up somewhere under `example`).

The structure for (2) is
- project.yml
- lib
      - build.sh
      - (any other files you need for your build)
- packages
  - sample
    - example
      - .include

where the file `.include` contains a single text line with `../../../lib/further-path-to-your-zip-file`.   In this case, the zip file must live somewhere under `lib`.

The structure for (3) is
- project.yml
- packages
  - sample
    - example
      - .include

and `.include` has the correct access path for the where your zip file ends up after the build (either form (1) or form (2) shown above).   You can omit `.include` entirely if and only if your zip file ends up being the only file in the the `example` directory (but I would encourage you to use `.include` anyway for clarity).

Note that `doctl` will recognize either `lib/build.sh` or `packages/sample/example/build.sh` as special and will run it (it should be marked executable).   It will run it in lieu of `npm install` even if there is a `package.json` because a user-supplied build script takes precedence.

Thanks for your answer @joshuaauerbachwatson!

I tested your options and here what I discover:

- `.include` file cannot contain relative path like `../../../lib/further-path-to-your-zip-file`, so I moved the zip folder inside `packages/sample/example` and leave the content of `.include` as `my-zip-file.zip`.
- `package.yml` should be modified to be able to find the entry point, in my zip file I had: `dist/index.js` exporting `main`, so my configuration inside `package.yml` becomes: `main: 'dist/index.main'`.

And that's it, everything works great!

For anyone who reach here and wants an example of what we talk, [see here](https://github.com/H4ad/serverless-adapter-examples/tree/master/examples/nestjs-digital-ocean) and example project with NestJS.

issues.body:
**What is the problem this feature would solve? Please describe.**

`doctl` aims to be useful in scripting. One way it does this is by providing a `--wait` flag for long running, async operations to block until until they are complete rather than making the user implement polling in their own script. Some examples include:

- `doctl compute droplet create --wait`
- `doctl kubernetes cluster create --wait`
- `doctl apps create --wait`

Currently the `doctl database create` command does not have a `--wait` flag.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Add a `--wait` flag to the `doctl database create` command. It should poll the [`/v2/databases/$DATABASE_ID` endpoint](https://docs.digitalocean.com/reference/api/api-reference/#operation/databases_get_cluster), blocking until the database cluster's `status` attribute moves from `creating` to `online`.

**Additional context**

Following the code path starting here demonstrates how `doctl apps create`'s  `--wait` flag is implemented:

https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/de1918ad1ee4b1e523c335fa9254e85d415d18aa/commands/apps.go#L282

One important difference for databases is that some database engines (mongodb now, but potentially others) only return the password in the initial response to the create request. It is _not_ included in subsequent GET responses. So that value must be retained.

Thanks for the traces.   They do make me suspicious that, at least in your case, the status command is looking for `credentials.json` under the snap install directory instead of your home directory, at least some of the time. I reproduced your trace for the `status` call on my ubuntu, and there is an interesting difference.   Where you have have

```
820  newfstatat(AT_FDCWD, "/snap/doctl/1064/opt/sandbox/creds/<hash>/credentials.json", 0xc0002982a8, 0) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
```

I have, instead, 
```
121188 newfstatat(AT_FDCWD, "/snap/doctl/1064/opt/sandbox/creds/<hash>/credentials.json", 0xc00022fa38, 0) = -1 EACCES (Permission denied)
```
The runs deviate after that point because (correctly) ENOENT is considered an error whereas (incorrectly) EACCES is ignored.

In other words
- there is a bug that we both suffer from: it should not be looking for credentials under `/snap`.   I can see the error in the code and I know how to fix it (in fact, I've coded the fix, the trick will be to test it).
- there is also a bug in handling errors from the status check, so that, in my case, the two bugs cancel but, (for some reason) in your case the returned error is the expected one and the first bug surfaces.

What I could still use your help with is in figuring out why there is a behavioral difference between our systems.  I'd like to understand this so as to be sure I'm not on the wrong track.   On my system:

```
ls /snap/doctl/1064/opt/sandbox/creds
```
gives a permission error (that is, `creds` has permissions 700, so the EACCES is to be expected).

How about on your system?  If that directory is searchable but does not contain a `credentials.json` then the ENOENT would then be expected.

@daniellionel01 thank you for this well documented report.

I believe there are actually two problems here.

1.  The message that is displayed when running a build is misleading.  It indeed omits part of the path.   I don't know how long that bug has been there but possibly a while .. it is easy not to notice as long as things are going well.   In fact, the build is not actually happening in the wrong directory (notice that when the failure is reported it is reported as happening in the expected directory). 
2.  When there are function builds and `doctl` is running under `snap`, you can get failures to find various tools that are, in fact, in your path.   I was able to reproduce this error in a linux image using a `snap` install.   As your transcript shows, `npm` was not found and so the build exited with a 127 code.   I believe this problem relates to the confined execution model that `snap` imposes.  I don't know a lot about `snap` and will need to get help with this part of the problem but obviously we should do something about it.

I will immediately open an internal ticket to fix problem (1).  It is not serious, in a sense, but will result in wasted effort attempting to debug the wrong problem.

To work around problem (2) while we're investigating exactly what to do about it you can
- use remote build:  `doctl sls deploy <dir> --remote-build`.   This will run the build in the runtime container.  I was able to circumvent the problem that way.
- install `doctl` by downloading the latest release from GitHub rather than by using `snap`.  I don't know if that's an option for you.

The problem of omitting the `/packages` segment from paths, when reporting build progress, is not in `doctl` proper but in another codebase incorporated via a plugin mechanism.   I have fixed that bug, but, because we are in the process of switching over the repository hosting for the other codebase, the fix will queue behind some other changes and may not appear in a `doctl` release immediately.   Note that the spurious message is _not_ related to the actual cause of the build failure.   I'm looking into that separately.
I was able to get it working with the "--remote-build" flag. Thanks for the quick response!

Unable to remove the label for the Kubernetes cluster node pool.

For adding a persistent node label to the Kubernetes worker nodes, we need to label the node pool using doctl. Once the label has been added how to remove it?

The documentation says the omitted labels will be removed. But how to remove the last label? 

For example, if we use the below command to add 3 labels to the node pool.

`doctl kubernetes cluster node-pool update <cluster name> <pool name/id> --label key1=value1,key2=value2,key3=value3`

We can remove the label key2=value2,key3=value3 using the below command
`doctl kubernetes cluster node-pool update <cluster name> <pool name/id> --label key1=value1`

But how to remove key1=value1  label? The below command doesn't work.
`doctl kubernetes cluster node-pool update <cluster name> <pool name/id> --label`

The label can be removed using the API call but using doctl it seems there isn't a way.
```
curl -X PUT \                                                                
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -d '{"name": "<node pool name> ","count": 3, "tags":["null"], "labels": {}}' \     
  "https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/kubernetes/clusters/<cluster ID>/node_pools/<node pool id>"
```

comment_details.body: There is a related CLI flag `--taint` where we solved this in one particular way. We could copy the pattern for labels.

Some extra context: the issue is that we use a `map[string]string` with an `omitempty` JSON tag in godo, meaning that an empty label map is not encoded.

A fix that does not involve a breaking change would require something like an extra field and/or a customer `json.Marshaler` implementation to handle the clear label case (possibly accompanied by a helper method). Details are to be determined.

Thank you for the question. The `--wait` command only waits for the droplet itself to boot (`Wait for Droplet creation to complete before returning`). As for your `user-data-file`, let me do some discovery on how we can `--wait` on this. I'll get back to you shortly.

@ChiefMateStarbuck thank you! 

At the moment, I am using effectively doing a `doctl compute ssh "$host" --ssh-command "tail -f /var/log/cloud-init-output.log" > "$logFile" &` and then tailing the log file and checking for `Cloud-init v. 22.2-0ubuntu1~18.04.3 finished` line before continuing.

Currently there is no way for doctl to know if a cloud-init script is in-progress. The `--wait` flag relies on the API reporting the Droplet as active. Knowing the status of cloud-init would require accessing the Droplet itself or an agent or other mechanism running on the Droplet.

You're current method is very close to what I generally recommend as a work around. One small improvement might be to use cloud-init's own status command rather than tailing the log. E.g. this would block until cloud-init completes:

    cloud-init status --wait

There is a bit of previous discussion here: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/issues/773
closed due to stale state.

comment_details.body:
Ok I haven't seen this documented anywhere but I was able to resolve this issue.

Turns out I had dependencies listed in my `package.json` file listed under `dependencies` and not `devDependencies`. I guess `doctl` is parsing the `package.json` file and if it sees anything under `dependencies` it creates a zip. Once I moved all of my deps under `devDependencies` everything was ok.

issues.body:
**Replication Steps**

When using doctl the default behavior of token auth, is to print the token to stdout per `<redacted>`.
```
doctl auth init -t $TOKEN

Using token [<redacted>]

Validating token... OK
```

This behavior is undesirable as the default behavior because security. 

**Desired Behavior**
No tokens or sensitive information are sent to stdout.

**Actual Behavior**
A sensitive token is printed to stdout which can be inadvertedly leaked.

**Reasoning**
Security. When doctl is used in CI (or other scenarios), it results in tokens being written to stdout which is often stored in a log state, creating opportunity for tokens to be leaked, unccessarily.

It is a requirement to authenticate docker with the DO registry via doctl, so it's a critical use case.

If this DX intended to help users verify their token, maybe default off and flag on with `--verify`?

Thanks for the great work on the CLI. Happy to offer any further feedback that will help 🤘

comment_details.body:
Hi @CollinAlpert. Sorry for the late response. 

It looks like you're on macOS, so I'm guessing your shell is zsh. If you were using bash, the example you provided would have worked as expected. Though in zsh, things work a bit differently:

> One commonly encountered difference is that variables substituted onto the command line are not split into words. See the description of the shell option `SH_WORD_SPLIT` in [Parameter Expansion](https://zsh.sourceforge.io/Doc/Release/Expansion.html#Parameter-Expansion). In zsh, you can either explicitly request the splitting (e.g. `${=foo}`) or use an array when you want a variable to expand to more than one word. See [Array Parameters](https://zsh.sourceforge.io/Doc/Release/Parameters.html#Array-Parameters).

https://zsh.sourceforge.io/Doc/Release/Roadmap.html

So if you use the following, it should do what you want:

    doctl registry repository delete-tag registry.digitalocean.com/<reg>/<repo> ${=TAGS}
Thanks for the explanation!

Hi @danaelhe I am working on this issue and noticed some inconsistencies in the APIs.

For the uptime alert `comparison` the values are either `greater_than` or `less_than` (see https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Adigitalocean%2Fopenapi%20greater_than&type=code).

But, the alert API is using `compare` with `GreaterThan` and `LessThan` (see https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Adigitalocean%2Fopenapi%20GreaterThan&type=code).

Should this be opened as a bug? The API spec is correct and I can hit the endpoints with the syntax, so I am assuming this would be in the actual API repo.

Oh yes, good catch. You are correct in that it is an inconsistency with the different types of `alert`s.  It is more of an inconsistency from a user experience perspective, as you point out, since functionally it's still accurate. Though, trying to enforce a common standard now would cause a breaking change. Unfortunately, it is not a breaking change we can fix right now. We will pass the feedback on to the appropriate internal product teams who will decide what/when is the best course of action to mitigate inconsistencies in the past and in the future.

Thank you for sharing your feedback!

issues.body:
**What is the problem this feature would solve? Please describe.**

This feature would solve the following problems & issues:

- No ability to run the following command in "offline" mode. For example:

      doctl app spec validate .do/app.yml --schema-only
      Error: Unable to initialize DigitalOcean API client: access token is required. (hint: run 'doctl auth init')

  - digitalocean/action-doctl#67
  - LyraPhase/docker-phasik.tv#5
- Security Risk: GitHub Actions using [digitalocean/action-doctl][1] for App Schema validation always requires an API `token`
  - The current action & implementation for `doctl app schema validate --schema-only ...` makes it impossible to follow the [principle of least priviledge][2]
  - This prevents [a proposed `no_auth` feature for digitalocean/action-doctl][3] from being currently possible.

[1]: https://github.com/digitalocean/action-doctl
[2]: https://securitylab.github.com/research/github-actions-building-blocks/#following-the-principle-of-least-privilege
[3]: https://github.com/trinitronx/action-doctl/pull/1

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Some way to validate a DigitalOcean App Spec in offline mode should be provided.  A separate command (e.g. `validate-offline`) should be decoupled from the `godo` API client & `auth` initialization to support this use case.

**Additional context**

Currently, the `doctl app spec validate` command is tightly coupled to require `godo` init and `doctl auth`.  The `validateCommand` is defined using [`CmdBuilder()`][4], which calls [`cmdBuilderWithInit(..., true, options...)`][5] with [`initCmd`][6] set to [`true` **always**][7] (This is passed to [`NewCmdConfig()`][8] as the [`initGodo` parameter which runs `cmdConfig.initServices()`][9]).

As such, the `--schema-only` flag still requires `doctl auth` and a `godo` client is initialized.  Unfortunately due to the way Cobra commands appear to be set up, the `--schema-only` flag is not available in the context where the command creation happens.  Therefore, it seems that we must implement a new sub-command for this feature (e.g. `doctl app spec validate-offline`). The usage of [`cmdBuilderWithInit` similar to this command PR][10] seems to be the proper method to setup this new command.

[4]: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/f6d249bcc18b0712bc8c3048c76addea25ec6b7d/commands/command.go#L66-L68
[5]: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/f6d249bcc18b0712bc8c3048c76addea25ec6b7d/commands/command.go#L70
[6]: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/f6d249bcc18b0712bc8c3048c76addea25ec6b7d/commands/command.go#L81C5-L81C12
[7]: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/f6d249bcc18b0712bc8c3048c76addea25ec6b7d/commands/command.go#L67C75-L67C79
[8]: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/f6d249bcc18b0712bc8c3048c76addea25ec6b7d/commands/command_config.go#L78
[9]: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/f6d249bcc18b0712bc8c3048c76addea25ec6b7d/commands/command_config.go#L193-L197
[10]: https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/pull/225

issues.body:
**What is the problem this feature would solve? Please describe.**
Currently `doctl` depends on `github.com/digitalocean/godo v1.121.0` but do not follow to use the replace directive declared in `godo's` go.mod as below.  Repo `godo` uses replace directive to pin `github.com/stretchr/objx` to version `v0.2.0` and `golang.org/x/crypto` to version `v0.0.0-20200420201142-3c4aac89819a`.

```
replace github.com/stretchr/objx => github.com/stretchr/objx v0.2.0
replace golang.org/x/crypto => golang.org/x/crypto v0.0.0-20200420201142-3c4aac89819a
```

According to [Go Modules wikis](https://go.dev/doc/modules/gomod-ref#replace-notes), `replace` directives in modules other than the main module are ignored when building the main module. It means such replace usage in go.mod cannot be inherited by downstream projects automatically.  Consequently, `doctl's` version of `github.com/stretchr/objx` and `golang.org/x/crypto` is different from the pinned version `github.com/digitalocean/godo` needed.

**Possible Solution.**
1. Remove the replace usage in `github.com/digitalocean/godo`.
2. Add the same replace rule to your go.mod
```
replace github.com/stretchr/objx => github.com/stretchr/objx v0.2.0
replace golang.org/x/crypto => golang.org/x/crypto v0.0.0-20200420201142-3c4aac89819a
```

**What is the problem this feature would solve? Please describe.**
doctl aims to be useful in scripting. One way it does this is by providing a --wait flag for long running, async operations to block until they are complete rather than making the user implement polling in their own script. Some examples include:

- `doctl database create --wait`
- `doctl compute droplet create --wait`
- `doctl kubernetes cluster create --wait`
- `doctl apps create --wait`

Currently the `doctl databases migrate` command does not have a `--wait` flag.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add a --wait flag to the `doctl databases migrate` command. It should poll the [/v2/databases/$DATABASE_ID/migrate](https://docs.digitalocean.com/reference/api/api-reference/#operation/databases_update_region), blocking until the database cluster's status attribute moves from migrating to online.

**Additional context**
Following the code path starting here demonstrates how `doctl database create`'s  `--wait` flag is implemented:

https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/de1918ad1ee4b1e523c335fa9254e85d415d18aa/commands/apps.go#L282

 --compression-type string            Specifies the compression type for a kafka topic: Possible values are 'producer', 'gzip', 'snappy', 'Iz4', 'zstd', 'uncompressed' (default "producer")
```

but in **doctl databases create** and most other places:

```
--engine pg                          The database's engine. Possible values are: pg, `mysql`, `redis`, `mongodb`, `kafka` and `opensearch`. (default "pg")
```

In the first example, apostrophes don't interfere with command argument type generation and it stays defined as **string**.
In the second example, backticks are causing to use first value (**pg**) as data type for argument, which can be confusing.

I would be happy to create PR to fix this, however, I am not sure whether there's any reason attached to using backticks versus apostrophes. I am also not sure why default value is in quotes.

One possible solution is to introduce **enum** data type, and then argument descriptions could look like this:

```
--engine enum                          The database's engine. Possible enum values are: `pg`, `mysql`, `redis`, `mongodb`, `kafka` and `opensearch`. (default "pg")
```

Digging through your code (sorry) I noticed that a part of setting up the serverless environment includes downloading Node v18. ```

To verify this, I can do a very dirty hack that's sure to give any Nix nerd reading this an aneurysm:

```
$ nix-shell -p nodejs_18
(... it downloads ... )

[nix-shell:~]$ rm ~/.config/doctl/sandbox/node

[nix-shell:~]$ ln -s "$(which node)" ~/.config/doctl/sandbox/node

[nix-shell:~]$ doctl serverless deploy sample-functions-python-helloworld --remote-build
Deploying '/home/ivan/Code/sample-functions-python-helloworld'
  to namespace 'fn-68c1b4e9-e5d4-4517-8b78-86c24ac6b7e8'

Another option I can think of is to wrap the `doctl` package in Nix with an overlay that also downloads Node v18 and symlinks it to where `doctl` expects it - the [`canReuseNode()` function](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/main/do/serverless.go#L1330) would pick up on it.

issues.body: ### Issue I'm utilizing the official [digitalocean/action-doctl@v2](https://github.com/digitalocean/action-doctl) Github action. I initialize the `doctl` client by passing an API key. I'm trying to create a droplet with the following `doctl` command: ``` doctl compute droplet create \ "$DROPLET_NAME" \ --region "nyc3" \ --size "s-1vcpu-1gb" \ --image "ubuntu-22-04-x64" \ --ssh-keys "$SSH_KEY" \ --project-id "$PROJECT_ID" \ --wait ``` This command successfully exits if I use an API key that has all permissions (`Full Access`). When I create & use an API key that only has the 4 CRUD permissions for `droplet`: I get the following error with exit code 1: ``` Error: POST https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/projects//resources: 403 (request "e1efed05-8592-491a-aeb3-e8bb968e6592") You are not authorized to perform this operation ``` Looking at the dashboard, I can verify that the droplet actually does end up being created. I've tried to guess the missing permissions by adding the `actions:read` permissions & `account:read` permissions with no success. According to the [official API reference docs](https://docs.digitalocean.com/reference/api/api-reference/#operation/droplets_create) `droplet:create` is the only permission required for creating droplets. The [official CLI reference docs](https://docs.digitalocean.com/reference/doctl/reference/compute/droplet/create/) doesn't provide any additional information on what API permissions are required to create a droplet. ### Question What is the narrowest set of API permissions I can use to successfully create (& exit code 0) a droplet using the CLI? **Environment:** - doctl version: `1.120.0 x64` - OS: `ubuntu-24.04` - OS Version: `20241215.1.0` - Installation method: Pre-installed via [digitalocean/action-doctl@v2](https://github.com/digitalocean/action-doctl). **Additional Details:** I'm running the example above as part of a pipeline in GitHub Actions.

comment_details.body:
After tinkering with API permission, it looks like we also need the `project:update` permission to successfully create a droplet via the CLI.

The documentation should probably get updated to reflect this fact.

@besirkurtulmus `project:update` is only required if you pass the `--project-id` flag. The API does not support specifying a project when creating a Droplet. So in doctl, when that flag is passed, we first create the Droplet and then call `POST /v2/projects/<uuid>/resources` to assign it to the desired project.

> @besirkurtulmus `project:update` is only required if you pass the `--project-id` flag. The API does not support specifying a project when creating a Droplet. Something is causing the `.Changed` field on the flag to not be set

It seems that the new `registries` command is what is causing this bug.
When `Registries()` builds the command, the flags of it's sub-commands map to the exact same names as those in the sub-commands created by `Registry()` for the `registry` command.
These flags are all written to a global table in the viper library (the `pflags` member of `var v *Viper` in `viper.go`).
So the flags created by `Registry()` are being overwritten by the `Registries()` flags.
The solution is to distinguish the generated flag names by the name of their parent command.

The empty string corresponds to "Use inbound user" in the DO Dashboard.

**Additional Details:**

Since the `--user` arg is not marked as a `requiredOpt()` in https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/c74c583764a12cc7ddb353acfe2733c5d20bc5d5/commands/databases.go#L1239-L1240

comment_details.body: Can I be assigned this issue to contribute?
! please assign

1) Explanation of the fix

We must detect whether the --user flag was explicitly passed. If it was passed we set req.User to the value the user provided (including "", so that --user "" results in empty string). If it was not passed we must not set the field, because the API expects the field to be optional and doctl should not force a value or raise an error.

Using Cobra's flag Changed boolean is reliable: it tells us whether the user actually passed the flag on the command line. This lets us support both:

doctl databases pool create ... (no --user → omit user from request),

doctl databases pool create ... --user "dbuser" (set user),

doctl databases pool create ... --user "" (explicitly set user to empty string — matches "Use inbound user").

2) Patch (replace the existing user-read block)

Find the location in doctl/commands/databases.go where the code currently reads the user:

// old (problematic) code
user, err := c.Doit.GetString(c.NS, doctl.ArgDatabasePoolUserName)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
req.User = user


Replace it with this updated block:

// new (fixed) code:
// Only set req.User if the user explicitly passed the --user flag.
// This allows omission (flag not provided) to mean "do not include the field"
// while still allowing explicit empty-string values (e.g. --user "").
if f := c.Cmd.Flags().Lookup(doctl.ArgDatabasePoolUserName); f != nil && f.Changed {
    user, err := c.Doit.GetString(c.NS, doctl.ArgDatabasePoolUserName)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    // Set req.User even if `user == ""`. An explicit empty string is meaningful
    // (represents "Use inbound user" in the Dashboard/API).
    req.User = user
}


Notes:

c.Cmd is the Cobra command instance available from the CmdConfig (c) passed to the handler. If your CmdConfig field is named differently, substitute accordingly.

Flags().Lookup(...).Changed is the standard Cobra API that indicates whether the flag was supplied in this invocation.

We keep c.Doit.GetString for proper parsing and viper integration, but only call it when the flag is actually present.

3) Test & Verification

Manual tests to run locally (after building the doctl binary from the updated source):

No user flag — should succeed (do not get the pool.create.user "missing arg" error):

doctl databases pool create <db-cluster-id> mypool --size 25 --db mydb --mode transaction


Expect: pool created; the CLI sends a payload without user field.

Explicit non-empty user:

doctl databases pool create <db-cluster-id> mypool --size 25 --db mydb --mode transaction --user dbuser


Expect: pool created; payload includes "user":"dbuser".

Explicit empty user:

doctl databases pool create <db-cluster-id> mypool --size 25 --db mydb --mode transaction --user ""


Expect: pool created; payload includes "user":"" (empty string) — this corresponds to "Use inbound user" behavior in the Dashboard.

Edge cases:

Short and long flag variants (if applicable).

Quoting rules for shells (some shells collapse --user "" — ensure quoting preserved).

Automated tests

If your test harness mocks the Do client, add tests to:

verify when flag not passed the request JSON does not contain user,

verify when flag passed empty string the request JSON contains "user":"",

verify when flag passed non-empty string that value is present.

4) Documentation

Update the help text and docs for doctl databases pool create to explicitly call out the following:

--user is optional.

If you explicitly pass --user "" (empty string) it sets the pool user to empty, which corresponds to the Dashboard option "Use inbound user" (N/A in table).

If you omit --user entirely, the field will be omitted from the API request and default behavior will be used.

A brief addition to the command help is helpful, e.g.:

AddStringFlag(cmdDatabasePoolCreate, doctl.ArgDatabasePoolUserName, "", "",
    "The username for the database user (optional). To use 'Use inbound user' behavior, pass --user \"\" explicitly.")

5) What I can do next

I can prepare a small PR patch (ready to apply) in the exact project layout with context lines if you want.

I can add unit tests that mock HTTP requests to verify the three behaviors (no flag / empty flag / non-empty flag).

I can update the help string in doctl/commands/databases.go and include a CHANGELOG note for release.

Would you like me to prepare the PR and include unit tests and documentation edits?
Please assign me this issue to implement the above plan

comment_details.body:
The fix is waiting for review after passing 3 checks...

Problem: Container Registry GET/DELETE API calls were failing for multi-registry operations.

Root Cause: The registriesService.ListRepositories method was incorrectly calling rs.client.Registry.ListRepositories instead of rs.client.Registries.ListRepositoriesV2, causing API endpoint mismatches.

issues.body:
### Description

All `doctl registry` subcommands (`repository list-v2`, `repository list-manifests`, `repository delete-manifest`, etc.) fail with an opaque 412 error when the account has multiple container registries, even though the `--registry` flag is documented as "optional."

This appears to be a server-side API change — these commands previously worked without `--registry`. There was no deprecation notice, changelog entry, or doctl release noting this breaking change.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a DigitalOcean account with multiple container registries
2. Run any registry command without `--registry`:

```bash
doctl registry repository list-v2 --output json
```

### Expected Behavior

Either:
- A clear CLI-level error message like: `Error: multiple registries found. Please specify one with --registry <name>. Available: reg1, reg2`
- Or the command prompts the user to select a registry

### Actual Behavior

Raw API error passed through:

```json
{
  "errors": [
    {
      "detail": "failed to get registry: GET https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/registry: 412 (request \"...\") This API is not supported if you have created multiple registries. Please use '/v2/registries/{registry_name}' instead. Refer to https://docs.digitalocean.com/reference/api/digitalocean/#tag/Container-Registry for more info."
    }
  ]
}
```

### Suggested Fix

- Detect multi-registry accounts in doctl and surface a user-friendly error with available registry names
- Update the `--registry` flag description — it's not truly "optional" for multi-registry accounts
- Document this as a breaking change for users who previously had a single registry and later created a second one

### Environment

- `doctl` version: 1.151.0 (also reproduced with 1.141.0 via `digitalocean/action-doctl@v2`)
- Affected commands: `registry get`, `registry repository list-v2`, `registry repository list-manifests`, `registry repository delete-manifest`, `registry garbage-collection start`

### Impact

This silently broke CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions cron jobs) that were using `doctl registry` commands without `--registry`. The workaround is to add `--registry <name>` to every command (or positional arg for `garbage-collection start`).

issues.body:
## Description

`doctl auth switch --context default` silently injects `default: "true"` into the `auth-contexts` map in `~/.config/doctl/config.yaml`. This entry is not a real token — it's a side effect of how `RunAuthSwitch` validates the requested context.

The bogus entry can break subsequent context switches because doctl may resolve the `default` context against `auth-contexts` (finding `"true"`) instead of the top-level `access-token`.

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Start with a clean config that has a named context
doctl auth init                              # sets top-level access-token
doctl auth init --context teamadf            # adds teamadf under auth-contexts

# Confirm no "default" key under auth-contexts
grep -A3 '^auth-contexts:' ~/.config/doctl/config.yaml

# Switch to default — this creates the bogus entry
doctl auth switch --context default

# Now check again
grep -A3 '^auth-contexts:' ~/.config/doctl/config.yaml
```

**Expected:**
```yaml
auth-contexts:
  teamadf: dop_v1_abc123...
```

**Actual:**
```yaml
auth-contexts:
  default: "true"
  teamadf: dop_v1_abc123...
```

The `default: "true"` entry appears every time you switch to the default context.

## Root cause

In [`commands/auth.go` → `RunAuthSwitch`](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/blob/main/commands/auth.go), the default context is temporarily added to the auth-contexts map for validation:

```go
contextsAvail := viper.GetStringMap("auth-contexts")
contextsAvail[doctl.ArgDefaultContext] = true
```

Later, viper's state (now containing `default: true`) is serialized back to the config file via `writeConfig()`. The temporary validation entry is never removed before the write.

## Impact

- The `default` context resolves to the string `"true"` instead of the top-level `access-token`, which can cause API calls to silently use the wrong token or fail.
- Users managing multiple contexts (e.g. switching between teams) get stale results because all contexts fall back to the same top-level token.
- The entry reappears after every `doctl auth switch --context default`, so manually removing it doesn't stick.

## Suggested fix

Remove the `default` key from the map after validation, before writing the config. Something like:

```go
contextsAvail := viper.GetStringMap("auth-contexts")
contextsAvail[doctl.ArgDefaultContext] = true  // for validation only

// ... validation logic ...

// Clean up before persisting
delete(contextsAvail, doctl.ArgDefaultContext)
```

## Workaround

Strip the bogus entry after switching:

```bash
# Wrapper function
doswitch() {
  local ctx="${1:-default}"
  doctl auth switch --context "$ctx"
  sed -i '/^  default: "true"$/d' "${HOME}/.config/doctl/config.yaml" 2>/dev/null
}
```

## Environment

- doctl version: 1.110.0-release
- OS: Linux (WSL2)
- Shell: bash

issues.body:
## Bug Report

### doctl version
`doctl version 1.152.0-release`

### Description

`doctl apps list-job-invocations <app-id> <job-name>` returns an empty table with no results, even when the job has many invocations recorded by the platform.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create an App Platform app with a scheduled job (kind: SCHEDULED)
2. Wait for the job to be invoked (either by the scheduler or manually)
3. Run `doctl apps list-job-invocations <app-id> <job-name>`

### Expected Behavior

The command should list all job invocations with their ID, phase, timestamps, etc.

### Actual Behavior

The command returns an empty table:

```
$ doctl apps list-job-invocations <app-id> cron-test
ID    Job Name    Created At    Started At    Completed At    Phase
```

However, the underlying API returns data correctly:

```
$ curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/apps/<app-id>/jobs/<job-name>/invocations" | python3 -m json.tool
```

Returns 13 invocations, all with `phase: SUCCEEDED`.

### Impact

This bug masked the real issue with our scheduled jobs — we spent hours thinking the cron scheduler was never firing, when in fact jobs were being invoked and failing. The empty CLI output made it appear that no invocations had ever occurred.

### Workaround

Use the API directly via `curl`.

### Environment
- OS: macOS (Darwin 24.2.0)
- doctl version: 1.152.0-release
- Shell: zsh

issues.body:
## Summary

doctl `v1.158.0` (released 2026-05-07 16:21 UTC) cannot read its own config files. Every doctl invocation fails at startup with:

```
doctl: 2026/05/07 21:08:20 Config initialization failed: While parsing config: yaml: line 2228: did not find expected key
```

`v1.157.0` reads the **same file** successfully — verified.

## Reproduction

1. Install doctl v1.158.0
2. Run any doctl command (auth init, auth list, registry login, etc.)
3. The first invocation may write a default config (37,883 bytes / 2,227 lines on Linux x86_64); subsequent invocations fail to read it.

The error appears at line 2228 of a 2227-line file — i.e., doctl's parser expects more YAML content than the writer produced. The file ends mid-section with `vpcs.update.name: ""`.

## Evidence the file itself is valid YAML

`yaml.safe_load` (PyYAML) parses the file successfully:
- 91 top-level keys
- Well-formed structure (1-click, access-token, account, action, activations, agent, alert, api-url, apikeys, apps, ...)

So the failure is in doctl's parser, not the file.

## Evidence v1.157.0 reads the same file

```bash
$ wget https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/releases/download/v1.157.0/doctl-1.157.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz
$ tar xf doctl-1.157.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz
$ ./doctl --config=/home/USER/.config/doctl/config.yaml auth list
default (current)        # <-- success on the same file v1.158.0 fails on
```

## Suspected commit

The v1.157.0 → v1.158.0 changelog has only 2 commits:

- [#1835 DOKS SSO: per-cluster config, kubeconfig type](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/pull/1835) — explicitly modifies config schema structure
- [#1839 Bump godo to v1.189.0](https://github.com/digitalocean/doctl/pull/1839) — internal HTTP client only, unlikely cause

#1835 is the prime suspect — config schema additions can produce serialization output that the parser doesn't expect.

## Impact

- All CI runs using `digitalocean/action-doctl@v2` (which defaults to `version: 'latest'`) broke today within hours of the v1.158.0 release.
- Workaround: pin to `version: '1.157.0'` in workflow input.
- Long-term users with shared doctl config homes (e.g., self-hosted runners) are affected even after pinning, since the broken file persists until manually cleared. v1.157.0 reads the v1.158.0-written file fine, so the workaround does not require config cleanup.

## Environment

- doctl: v1.158.0
- OS: Ubuntu (self-hosted GitHub Actions runner, Linux x86_64)
- Action: `digitalocean/action-doctl@v2` with `version: 'latest'` (default)

## Workaround applied on our side

Pinning `version: '1.157.0'` in all `digitalocean/action-doctl@v2` callsites until v1.159.0 (or v1.158.x) ships a fix.

Happy to provide the corrupted config file (with secrets redacted) on request.
